title: Syllabus
text:
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Choose a tracking technology appropriate to a species, a question and a budget, and state its biases and its ethical constraints.
Handle spatial and movement data in R — import, reproject, clean, visualise — without hand-waving about coordinate reference systems.
Quantify a trajectory: step lengths, turning angles, speeds, net displacement, and space use (MCP, KDE, AKDE).
Annotate a trajectory with remotely sensed environmental covariates, matched in space and in time.
Segment a trajectory into behavioural states with a hidden Markov model and interpret the output critically.
Fit and interpret resource selection and step selection functions, including the availability decisions that drive their conclusions.
Work reproducibly: scripted analyses that another person — including future you — can rerun.

Pop quizzes
Multiple-choice questions are embedded directly in the slides. Click an option and the deck reveals the correct answer(s) and a short explanation. They are not graded — they exist so that you, and I, find out in real time whether an idea landed. Answer honestly; a wrong answer in class is free, a wrong answer in the exam is not.


Exercises
Every class has a companion exercise page with the full R code. Solutions are in collapsible blocks: try first, then unfold. The exercises are cumulative — the object you build in Class 3 is the object you model in Class 8.

title: Syllabus
text:
Assessment
The course is worth 2 CFU and is assessed on a short reproducible project rather than a written exam:

Pick one of the course datasets (or bring your own, with my approval).
Pose one clear question that the data can answer.
Produce a Quarto document (~4–6 pages rendered) containing: the question, the data-cleaning steps, one or two analyses drawn from the course, the figures, and an honest paragraph on the limitations.
Submit the .qmd and the rendered HTML, so that the analysis can be rerun.

Assessment weights: correctness of the analysis (40%), justification of the methodological choices (30%), reproducibility and code clarity (20%), clarity of the figures and writing (10%).






Note



The most common way to lose marks is to run an analysis whose assumptions the data violate — for example fitting an HMM to a track with wildly irregular sampling intervals without addressing it. Saying “this is a limitation because X” earns marks; silently ignoring it does not.

title: Syllabus
text:
Prerequisites
No prior R experience is assumed, but the pace is brisk. If you have never opened R, work through the setup page before Class 1 and budget an evening for the linked introductory tutorial. Basic ecology and statistics (regression, likelihood, the idea of a probability distribution) are assumed.

title: Datasets
text:
1. African buffalo, Kruger National Park
data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz
Six GPS-collared buffalo (Syncerus caffer) in Kruger National Park, South Africa, 2005–2006. Collars reported roughly hourly. This is our workhorse dataset: several individuals, a long series, a confined landscape with strong environmental gradients (rivers, vegetation).






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: duplicates



The raw file contains 3,747 rows that duplicate an existing individual + timestamp combination — about 13% of the file. These come from the tag transmitting the same fix more than once. If you compute step lengths without removing them you get a large number of zero-length steps in zero elapsed time, and your speed distribution acquires an infinite tail.
We fix this properly in Class 3.


Used in: Classes 3, 4, 5, 7, 8.
Source: Getz WM, Fortmann-Roe S, Cross PC, Lyons AJ, Ryan SJ, Wilmers CC. Movebank study Kruger African Buffalo, GPS tracking, South Africa.

title: Datasets
text:
2. Parti-coloured bat, Switzerland
data/bat_safi.csv.gz
Seventeen bats (Vespertilio murinus) tracked by VHF radio-telemetry near Bern, Switzerland, 2002–2003. Only 1,740 fixes in total.






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: small, irregular, hand-collected data



This is what tracking looked like before GPS, and what it still looks like for any animal too small to carry a satellite tag. Fixes arrive when a human with an antenna managed to get a bearing — so intervals are wildly irregular, nights are dense and days are empty, and individuals have between a handful and a few hundred locations.
Most of the methods in this course assume regular sampling. Applying them here without thinking produces confident nonsense — which is exactly why we use this dataset to practise saying “no, not with these data”.


Used in: Classes 3, 4 (as a cautionary counter-example).
Source: Safi K, et al. Movebank study Parti-colored bat Safi Switzerland.

title: Datasets
text:
3. Turkey vulture “Leo”
data/vulture_leo.csv.gz
A single turkey vulture (Cathartes aura) called Leo, tracked by GPS for almost six years (2007–2013) between Canada and Venezuela — over 60° of latitude.






ImportantThe lesson this dataset teaches: one animal, many behaviours



Leo is not doing one thing. He has breeding-ground residency, autumn migration, wintering residency, and spring migration, repeated over six annual cycles. A single home range estimate over the whole track is meaningless — it would describe a “range” covering two continents.
This is the dataset for Class 6: a trajectory that demands segmentation before any other analysis makes sense. It also crosses many UTM zones, which makes it a good test of whether you have understood projections.


Used in: Classes 4, 6.
Source: Bildstein K, Barber D, Bechard MJ. Movebank study Turkey Vulture Acopian Center USA GPS.

title: Datasets
text:
Movebank column conventions
Movebank exports share a vocabulary. When R reads the CSV, hyphens in the header become dots, so location-long becomes location.long.






Column
Meaning



event.id
Unique id of this record


timestamp
Fix time, UTC, YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.sss




location.long, location.lat

Longitude / latitude, decimal degrees, WGS84 (EPSG:4326)



individual.local.identifier
The animal’s name or code — your grouping variable


tag.local.identifier
The device — not the same as the animal


individual.taxon.canonical.name
Species


sensor.type

gps, radio-transmitter, argos-doppler-shift, …


visible

false = flagged as bad by the data owner


manually.marked.outlier

true = flagged by hand as an outlier



study.local.timestamp, study.timezone

Local time, if you need day/night









TipTwo habits worth forming now



Always keep timestamp in UTC for computation and convert to local time only for interpretation. Mixing the two is the single most common source of silent errors in movement analysis.
Never assume individual == tag. Tags get redeployed on different animals, and animals get recollared. Group by the individual.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Goals. Generate random steps and look inside a stratum; fit an SSF; add movement terms for a full iSSA; update and interpret the movement kernel; add a habitat × movement interaction; discover why covariate resolution decides whether any of this works; and fit all six animals.
Time: ~55 minutes. Packages: amt, terra, survival, dplyr, tidyr, lubridate.
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(lubridate)

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Setup

clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

covs <- project(
  c(rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif"), rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")),
  "EPSG:32736"
)
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"    "cropland"
round(res(covs))
#> [1] 893 893







Note



Note the pixel size: 893 m. Remember that number — it decides the outcome of this entire exercise.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 1 — Build the strata

steps_for <- function(animal, rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(15)) {
  trk |>
    filter(id == animal) |>
    track_resample(rate = rate, tolerance = tolerance) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) |>
    steps_by_burst() |>
    filter(sl_ < 10000)          # drop the spatial outliers found in Class 3
}

set.seed(2026)
obs <- steps_for("Cilla")

ssf_dat <- obs |>
  random_steps(n_control = 15) |>
  extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")

c(strata = n_distinct(ssf_dat$step_id_), rows = nrow(ssf_dat))
#> strata   rows 
#>   3512  56192
names(ssf_dat)
#>  [1] "burst_"          "x1_"             "x2_"             "y1_"            
#>  [5] "y2_"             "sl_"             "ta_"             "t1_"            
#>  [9] "t2_"             "dt_"             "case_"           "step_id_"       
#> [13] "elevation_start" "trees_start"     "grassland_start" "shrubs_start"   
#> [17] "cropland_start"  "elevation_end"   "trees_end"       "grassland_end"  
#> [21] "shrubs_end"      "cropland_end"

Your turn
1a. Look inside a single stratum. What varies within it, and what does not? 1b. Why does where = "both" give you _start and _end columns?






NoteSolution






ssf_dat |>
  filter(step_id_ == ssf_dat$step_id_[1]) |>
  transmute(case_, sl_ = round(sl_), ta_ = round(ta_, 2),
            elevation_start = round(elevation_start),
            elevation_end = round(elevation_end),
            grassland_end = round(grassland_end, 2)) |>
  head(16)
#> # A tibble: 16 × 6
#>    case_   sl_   ta_ elevation_start elevation_end grassland_end
#>  * <lgl> <dbl> <dbl>           <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#>  1 TRUE    594  0.87             258           272          0.82
#>  2 FALSE    49 -1.11             258           258          0.92
#>  3 FALSE   487 -0.2              258           258          0.92
#>  4 FALSE   339 -0.32             258           258          0.92
#>  5 FALSE   287  0.78             258           270          0.87
#>  6 FALSE    55 -0.94             258           258          0.92
#>  7 FALSE   537  2.2              258           270          0.87
#>  8 FALSE   126 -2.85             258           258          0.92
#>  9 FALSE   246 -1.5              258           258          0.92
#> 10 FALSE     3  2.48             258           258          0.92
#> 11 FALSE   580 -0.16             258           258          0.92
#> 12 FALSE   147  0.85             258           258          0.92
#> 13 FALSE    35  0.49             258           258          0.92
#> 14 FALSE    20  0.98             258           258          0.92
#> 15 FALSE    83  1.87             258           270          0.87
#> 16 FALSE     6 -0.28             258           258          0.92

Within a stratum: one row with case_ = TRUE (the step the animal took) and 15 with case_ = FALSE (steps it could have taken). The start point, the time, the animal and everything else about that moment are identical — only the destination, and hence the _end covariates, vary.
That is the whole design. Because the likelihood compares only within strata, every time-constant confounder cancels: hour of day, season, weather, the animal’s identity, its internal state. You get that control for free.
where = "both" extracts covariates at the start and end of each step. You need both: _end covariates express selection (where did it go), _start covariates modify the movement kernel (how does it move when starting from here). Task 5 uses that distinction.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 2 — A basic SSF

m_ssf <- fit_issf(
  ssf_dat,
  case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end + strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_ssf$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.0102    0.9899   0.0023 -4.5012   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0245    0.9758   0.2942 -0.0831   0.9338

Your turn
2a. Interpret the coefficients.






NoteSolution





Coefficients are on the log scale, exactly as for an RSF, and there is no intercept. exp(coef) is the relative selection strength: the factor by which the relative probability of choosing a step multiplies per unit increase in the covariate, compared with the other steps available at that moment.
Elevation is measured in metres, so its coefficient is per metre — small by construction. Standardise if you want comparable effect sizes:

zs <- ssf_dat |>
  mutate(across(c(elevation_end, grassland_end), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))))

m_z <- fit_issf(zs, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end + strata(step_id_),
                model = TRUE)
round(summary(m_z$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.3189    0.7270   0.0708 -4.5012   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0033    0.9967   0.0403 -0.0831   0.9338

Elevation is strongly and clearly negative. Grassland — the covariate that mattered most in Class 7 — is indistinguishable from zero. Hold that thought.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 3 — A full iSSA
Add the movement terms so that the movement kernel is estimated jointly with selection.

m_issa <- fit_issf(
  ssf_dat,
  case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
          strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_issa$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> elevation_end -0.0102    0.9898   0.0022 -4.5558   0.0000
#> grassland_end -0.0232    0.9770   0.2926 -0.0794   0.9367
#> sl_            0.0000    1.0000   0.0001  0.2731   0.7848
#> log(sl_)       0.0052    1.0052   0.0128  0.4037   0.6865
#> cos(ta_)       0.0058    1.0058   0.0269  0.2159   0.8291

Your turn
3a. Recover the realised movement kernel and compare it with the tentative one.






NoteSolution






tent_sl <- sl_distr(ssf_dat)
tent_ta <- ta_distr(ssf_dat)

upd_sl <- update_gamma(
  tent_sl,
  beta_sl     = coef(m_issa)[["sl_"]],
  beta_log_sl = coef(m_issa)[["log(sl_)"]]
)
upd_ta <- update_vonmises(tent_ta, beta_cos_ta = coef(m_issa)[["cos(ta_)"]])

data.frame(
  quantity = c("gamma shape", "gamma scale", "mean step (m)", "vonMises kappa"),
  tentative = round(c(tent_sl$params$shape, tent_sl$params$scale,
                      tent_sl$params$shape * tent_sl$params$scale,
                      tent_ta$params$kappa), 3),
  realised  = round(c(upd_sl$params$shape, upd_sl$params$scale,
                      upd_sl$params$shape * upd_sl$params$scale,
                      upd_ta$params$kappa), 3)
)
#>         quantity tentative realised
#> 1    gamma shape     0.607    0.612
#> 2    gamma scale   467.829  471.761
#> 3  mean step (m)   283.740  288.558
#> 4 vonMises kappa     0.717    0.723

The tentative distribution is the one random_steps() fitted to the observed steps and sampled the controls from. The realised kernel is what the animal actually does once selection is accounted for.
Here they are almost identical, and the movement coefficients are non-significant — meaning that for this animal, at this interval, habitat is not detectably distorting the movement kernel.






Tip



Do this arithmetic with update_gamma() / update_vonmises(), never by hand. The relationship between the coefficients and the distribution parameters depends on the parameterisation, and getting it wrong is easy and silent.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 4 — Why grassland vanished
Class 7 found grassland to be the strongest covariate. Here it is nothing. Something is wrong — and it is not the biology.

# How often does a control step land in the SAME raster cell as the start?
mean(ssf_dat$grassland_end == ssf_dat$grassland_start, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.6928025
median(obs$sl_)
#> [1] 150.1476
round(res(covs)[1])
#> [1] 893







ImportantThe step is smaller than the pixel



The median hourly step is about 150 m. The land-cover cells are 893 m across. So roughly 69% of control steps land in the very same cell as the step’s origin — the used step and its alternatives are assigned identical covariate values, and the stratum contains no contrast for the model to exploit.
An SSF can only detect selection for a covariate that varies within the animal’s reach in one time step. If your pixels are bigger than your steps, you will find nothing, no matter how strong the real preference is.


Your turn
4a. Refit at 3- and 6-hourly intervals and watch the effect appear.






NoteSolution






compare_rates <- lapply(c(1, 3, 6), function(h) {
  o <- steps_for("Cilla", rate = hours(h), tolerance = minutes(15))
  set.seed(1)
  d <- o |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")
  f <- fit_issf(d, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
                  sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_), model = TRUE)
  cc <- summary(f$model)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    interval_h  = h,
    strata      = n_distinct(d$step_id_),
    median_sl_m = round(median(o$sl_)),
    same_cell   = round(mean(d$grassland_end == d$grassland_start, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    grass_beta  = round(cc["grassland_end", "coef"], 3),
    grass_p     = round(cc["grassland_end", "Pr(>|z|)"], 4)
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

compare_rates
#>   interval_h strata median_sl_m same_cell grass_beta grass_p
#> 1          1   3512         150      0.69     -0.055  0.8535
#> 2          3   1172         478      0.43      0.220  0.5417
#> 3          6    584         934      0.21      0.648  0.1293


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(compare_rates$interval_h, compare_rates$same_cell, type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Sampling interval (h)", ylab = "Fraction of controls in the start cell",
     main = "Contrast available to the model")
plot(compare_rates$interval_h, compare_rates$grass_beta, type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#c1440e", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Sampling interval (h)", ylab = "Grassland coefficient",
     main = "...and the effect it can detect")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

As the interval lengthens, steps get longer, controls reach further, fewer land in the origin cell — and the grassland coefficient climbs from essentially zero to a substantial positive value, recovering the selection Class 7 detected.






WarningDo not read this as “longer intervals are better”



You are trading one bias for another. Longer steps give more spatial contrast, but they also coarsen the behavioural question: a 6-hour “step” is a straight line drawn across six hours of real movement, and it no longer represents a single movement decision.
The honest conclusion is that 893 m land cover is the wrong resolution for hourly buffalo data. The fix is finer covariates — Sentinel-2 at 10–20 m would resolve this comfortably — not a coarser animal.
The general rule: your covariate resolution must be finer than your typical step length, or the step selection design has nothing to compare.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 5 — Habitat × movement interactions
Does the animal move differently depending on where it starts? Use the 6-hourly data, where there is contrast to work with.

obs6 <- steps_for("Cilla", rate = hours(6), tolerance = minutes(30))
set.seed(7)
d6 <- obs6 |> random_steps(n_control = 20) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")

m_int <- fit_issf(
  d6,
  case_ ~ grassland_end + elevation_end +
          sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) +
          sl_:grassland_start +
          cos(ta_):grassland_start +
          strata(step_id_),
  model = TRUE
)

round(summary(m_int$model)$coefficients, 4)
#>                             coef exp(coef) se(coef)       z Pr(>|z|)
#> grassland_end             0.4761    1.6098   0.4244  1.1219   0.2619
#> elevation_end            -0.0145    0.9856   0.0033 -4.4284   0.0000
#> sl_                      -0.0006    0.9994   0.0003 -1.7349   0.0828
#> log(sl_)                 -0.0211    0.9791   0.0824 -0.2559   0.7980
#> cos(ta_)                 -1.9353    0.1444   0.4190 -4.6183   0.0000
#> sl_:grassland_start       0.0007    1.0007   0.0003  1.9028   0.0571
#> cos(ta_):grassland_start  2.2115    9.1297   0.4689  4.7169   0.0000

Your turn
5a. Interpret the two interaction terms.






NoteSolution





The two interactions answer different questions from the selection terms:


sl_:grassland_start — does the animal take longer steps when it starts in grassland? A positive coefficient means it moves faster through grassland; a negative one means it slows down and lingers, which is what you would expect where it feeds.

cos(ta_):grassland_start — does it move more directionally from grassland? Positive means straighter paths; negative means more tortuous, the signature of area-restricted search.

Note carefully that these use grassland_**start**, the habitat at the origin of the step. A common and serious error is to interact sl_ with grassland_end, which is not a movement statement at all — it conditions on the destination and mangles the interpretation of both terms.
The combination is what makes iSSA worth the trouble: an RSF has no movement component, so “goes there” and “behaves differently there” collapse into a single undifferentiated measure of use.
What these particular numbers say
Both interactions come out positive, and cos(ta_) has a large negative main effect. Read them together:


Turning. The main effect (cos(ta_) ≈ −1.9) applies where grassland_start = 0: away from grassland the animal’s movement is strongly anti-persistent — it reverses direction, staying in a small area. Adding the interaction (≈ +2.2) gives roughly +0.3 in pure grassland: from grassland, movement is mildly directional.

Step length. sl_:grassland_start is positive: steps starting in grassland are longer.

So at this six-hour scale the picture is the opposite of a foraging-patch story: buffalo tend to move into grassland (grassland_end positive, though imprecise) but cross it in long, straight steps, while their movement off grassland is short and tortuous — consistent with grassland acting as a travel matrix and the wooded/riverine areas as places to settle.






Warning



Do not over-read this. grassland_end here is not statistically distinguishable from zero for a single animal, and a six-hour step is a coarse summary of movement. It is an interpretation to take to Task 6 and test across individuals, not a conclusion.

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Task 6 — All six animals

fit_animal <- function(animal) {
  o <- steps_for(animal, rate = hours(6), tolerance = minutes(30))
  if (nrow(o) < 100) return(NULL)
  set.seed(11)
  d <- o |> random_steps(n_control = 15) |> extract_covariates(covs, where = "both")
  f <- try(fit_issf(d, case_ ~ elevation_end + grassland_end +
                      sl_ + log(sl_) + cos(ta_) + strata(step_id_),
                    model = TRUE), silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(f, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  cc <- summary(f$model)$coefficients
  data.frame(id = animal, term = rownames(cc), beta = cc[, "coef"])
}

per_animal <- lapply(unique(trk$id), fit_animal) |> bind_rows()

per_animal |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = id, values_from = beta) |>
  mutate(across(-term, \(z) signif(z, 3)))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   term                Queen       Gabs      Cilla      Mvubu       Toni   Pepper
#>   <chr>               <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 elevation_end -0.00207    -0.0163    -0.0165    -0.0194    -0.00359   -1.63e-2
#> 2 grassland_end  1.01        0.158      0.65       0.308     -1.01       7.69e-1
#> 3 sl_            0.00000843  0.0000163 -0.0000142 -0.0000053 -0.0000297  4.54e-5
#> 4 log(sl_)      -0.0314      0.00911    0.0422     0.0328     0.0127     6.08e-3
#> 5 cos(ta_)       0.0129      0.00543    0.0231     0.00363   -0.00912   -1.15e-2







Tip



sl_ is measured per metre, so its coefficient is tiny by construction and rounds to zero at three decimals — signif() rather than round() keeps it readable. This is a presentation problem, not a modelling one, but it is worth handling before anyone concludes the effect is exactly zero.


Your turn
6a. Summarise across individuals. Which effects are consistent?






NoteSolution






pop <- per_animal |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(n_animals = n(),
            mean_beta = mean(beta),
            se = sd(beta) / sqrt(n()),
            t = mean_beta / se,
            p = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n() - 1),
            n_positive = sum(beta > 0),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_beta, se, t), \(z) round(z, 3)), p = round(p, 4))

pop
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   term          n_animals mean_beta    se      t      p n_positive
#>   <chr>             <int>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 cos(ta_)              6     0.004 0.005  0.763 0.480           4
#> 2 elevation_end         6    -0.012 0.003 -4.04  0.0099          0
#> 3 grassland_end         6     0.313 0.293  1.07  0.334           5
#> 4 log(sl_)              6     0.012 0.01   1.14  0.305           5
#> 5 sl_                   6     0     0      0.327 0.757           3


boxplot(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        las = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "Coefficient",
        main = "iSSA coefficients, 6 buffalo (6-hourly)")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
stripchart(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6), cex = 0.9)







Read the n_positive column alongside the p-value. With six animals, a term with the same sign in 6 of 6 is strong evidence of a consistent population-level effect even when the mean is imprecise; one that is positive in 3 and negative in 3 is not a population effect however narrow its interval.
This two-stage summary is honest about sample size: your degrees of freedom come from the number of animals, not the hundreds of thousands of rows in the strata.
With more individuals you would move to a mixed conditional model — glmmTMB with random slopes and the stratum-intercept variance fixed large, following Muff et al. (2020).

title: Exercise 8 — Step selection and iSSA
text:
Self-check

Suppose an iSSA reported a positive coefficient on grassland_end and a negative one on sl_:grassland_start (note: not the pattern our buffalo showed). What would the animal be doing?

Avoiding grassland but crossing it quickly
Moving into grassland, then slowing down once there
Taking longer steps towards grassland
The two results contradict each other


Two different statements, and they fit together neatly.
grassland_end positive: among the steps available at each moment, the animal chooses those ending in grassland — selection.
sl_:grassland_start negative: when it starts a step in grassland, that step is shorter — it slows down.
Together: the animal heads into grassland and then lingers there. That is the classic signature of a foraging patch, and it is exactly what a large grazer should do.
An RSF cannot express this at all: it has no movement component, so “goes there” and “slows down there” collapse into one undifferentiated measure of use.



You have Argos locations with 1–5 km error and a 30 m land-cover map. Should you fit an iSSA?

Yes — 30 m resolution gives excellent covariate contrast
No — the positional error is far larger than the covariate grain, so the covariate assigned to each step is essentially random
Yes, but only with more control steps
Yes, after projecting everything to UTM


With kilometres of positional error, you do not know which 30 m cell the animal was in — the land-cover value you extract is close to a random draw from a large neighbourhood. Fine covariates cannot rescue coarse locations; they just add noise with a confident-looking resolution.
This is the mirror image of Task 4. There the pixels were too coarse relative to the steps; here they are too fine relative to the location error. Both break the same requirement:

the covariate must vary meaningfully at the scale you can actually resolve the animal’s position and movement.

With Argos data, aggregate the covariates to something comparable to the error (1–5 km), and ask a broader-scale question — an RSF at second order, not an iSSA.

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
text:
Goals. Build used and available samples; fit an RSF and read the coefficients as odds ratios; check that estimates stabilise as availability grows; change the availability domain and watch the answer move; fit all six buffalo two-stage; and map the predicted selection surface.
Time: ~55 minutes. Packages: amt, terra, sf, dplyr, tidyr.
library(amt)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
text:
Setup

clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

# Covariates, projected to match the track
elev <- rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif")
terr <- terrain(elev, v = c("slope", "TRI"), unit = "degrees")
names(terr) <- c("slope", "tri")
lc <- rast("data/kruger_landcover.tif")

covs <- project(c(elev, terr, lc), "EPSG:32736")
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "slope"     "tri"       "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"   
#> [7] "cropland"







WarningProject the covariates once, at the start



The track is in UTM 36S. amt’s extract_covariates() will not reproject for you — hand it a raster in EPSG:4326 and every covariate comes back NA, and glm() then fails with no (non-missing) observations. Project once, here, and the rest of the exercise just works.

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
text:
Task 1 — Used and available

set.seed(2026)

cilla <- trk |> filter(id == "Cilla")

rsf_dat <- cilla |>
  random_points(n = nrow(cilla) * 10) |>
  extract_covariates(covs)

table(rsf_dat$case_)
#> 
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#> 35280  3528
mean(is.na(rsf_dat$elevation))
#> [1] 0

random_points() applied to a track draws available points inside that animal’s MCP — so this is a third-order analysis: where does Cilla go within the range she has already chosen?
Your turn
1a. Standardise the covariates and add the infinite weights. 1b. Why weight the available points so heavily?






NoteSolution






covars <- c("elevation", "slope", "tri", "trees", "grassland", "shrubs")

d <- rsf_dat |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
  mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
         w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

nrow(d)
#> [1] 38808

The used–available design is really an inhomogeneous Poisson point process, and logistic regression is a computational device for fitting it. The equivalence is exact only in the limit of infinitely many, infinitely down-weighted available points. Giving the available points a large weight (here 5,000) makes the logistic coefficients converge to the correct point-process coefficients.
Standardising makes the coefficients comparable across covariates measured in different units — “per one standard deviation” — and improves the numerical conditioning of the fit.

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
text:
Task 2 — Fit and interpret

fit <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
           data = d, family = binomial(), weights = w)

round(summary(fit)$coefficients, 4)
#>             Estimate Std. Error   z value Pr(>|z|)
#> (Intercept) -10.8483     0.0173 -628.3246   0.0000
#> elevation     0.1425     0.0210    6.7763   0.0000
#> slope         0.2920     0.0218   13.4035   0.0000

Your turn
2a. Express each coefficient as an odds ratio with a confidence interval. 2b. Which covariate has the strongest effect, and in which direction?






NoteSolution






res <- data.frame(
  term = names(coef(fit)),
  beta = coef(fit),
  se   = summary(fit)$coefficients[, 2]
) |>
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") |>
  mutate(
    RSS   = round(exp(beta), 2),                       # relative selection strength
    lower = round(exp(beta - 1.96 * se), 2),
    upper = round(exp(beta + 1.96 * se), 2),
    beta  = round(beta, 3)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(beta)))

res
#>                term   beta         se  RSS lower upper
#> grassland grassland -0.477 0.08958078 0.62  0.52  0.74
#> shrubs       shrubs -0.296 0.05277846 0.74  0.67  0.82
#> slope         slope  0.292 0.02178613 1.34  1.28  1.40
#> tri             tri -0.210 0.02968249 0.81  0.76  0.86
#> elevation elevation  0.143 0.02103398 1.15  1.11  1.20
#> trees         trees -0.045 0.05109606 0.96  0.87  1.06


r <- res[order(res$beta), ]
plot(r$beta, seq_len(nrow(r)), pch = 16, col = "#1f6f78", cex = 1.3,
     xlim = range(c(r$beta - 1.96 * r$se, r$beta + 1.96 * r$se)),
     yaxt = "n", ylab = "", xlab = "Coefficient (log scale, per 1 SD)",
     main = "Cilla: third-order selection")
segments(r$beta - 1.96 * r$se, seq_len(nrow(r)),
         r$beta + 1.96 * r$se, seq_len(nrow(r)), col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2)
axis(2, at = seq_len(nrow(r)), labels = r$term, las = 1, cex.axis = 0.8)
abline(v = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)







Read the table as relative selection strength: RSS = exp(beta) is the factor by which the relative probability of use multiplies for a one-standard- deviation increase in that covariate, holding the others fixed.
An RSS of 1 means no selection; the confidence interval tells you whether you can distinguish it from 1.
Note the intercept is not interpretable. It absorbs the arbitrary ratio of available to used points — change n and the intercept moves, while the slopes do not. That is precisely why only relative statements are licensed.

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
section: Task 3 — Does availability sample size matter?
text:
Task 3 — Does availability sample size matter?
The number of available points is your choice. The estimates should stop moving once you have drawn enough.

multipliers <- c(1, 5, 10, 25, 50)

stab <- lapply(multipliers, function(m) {
  dd <- cilla |>
    random_points(n = nrow(cilla) * m) |>
    extract_covariates(covs) |>
    filter(if_all(all_of(covars), \(z) !is.na(z))) |>
    mutate(across(all_of(covars), \(z) as.numeric(scale(z))),
           w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))
  f <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
           data = dd, family = binomial(), weights = w)
  data.frame(mult = m,
             term = names(coef(f))[-1],
             beta = as.numeric(coef(f))[-1],
             se   = summary(f)$coefficients[-1, 2])
}) |> bind_rows()

stab |>
  select(mult, term, beta) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mult, values_from = beta) |>
  mutate(across(-term, \(z) round(z, 3)))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   term         `1`    `5`   `10`   `25`   `50`
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 elevation  0.171  0.128  0.14   0.128  0.136
#> 2 slope      0.374  0.268  0.266  0.272  0.265
#> 3 tri       -0.24  -0.152 -0.176 -0.191 -0.187
#> 4 trees     -0.1   -0.045 -0.089 -0.088 -0.082
#> 5 grassland -0.613 -0.444 -0.536 -0.524 -0.535
#> 6 shrubs    -0.405 -0.273 -0.322 -0.316 -0.33

Your turn
3a. Have the coefficients stabilised? 3b. What happens to the standard errors?






NoteSolution






par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

terms <- unique(stab$term)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(terms), "Dark 3")
plot(range(multipliers), range(stab$beta), type = "n", log = "x",
     xlab = "Available points (× n used)", ylab = "Coefficient",
     main = "Estimates stabilise")
for (i in seq_along(terms)) {
  z <- stab[stab$term == terms[i], ]
  lines(z$mult, z$beta, col = cols[i], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 16)
}
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
legend("bottomright", terms, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.6)

plot(range(multipliers), range(stab$se), type = "n", log = "xy",
     xlab = "Available points (× n used)", ylab = "Standard error",
     main = "SEs shrink without limit")
for (i in seq_along(terms)) {
  z <- stab[stab$term == terms[i], ]
  lines(z$mult, z$se, col = cols[i], lwd = 2, type = "b", pch = 16)
}






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The coefficients settle down: past roughly 10× the used sample they barely move, which is the check you should always run and report.
The standard errors keep shrinking as you add available points — and this is the crucial asymmetry. Availability points carry information about the landscape, not about the animal. Drawing more of them makes your estimate of what was available more precise, so the SEs fall, but you have not observed the animal any more closely.
That is why p-values in used–available designs are close to meaningless: you choose the sample size, so you choose the p-value. Report effect sizes, confidence intervals, consistency across individuals, and validation.

  population_mcp_km2 = round(hr_area(pop_mcp)$area / 1e6))

          data = third, family = binomial(), weights = w)
f2 <- glm(case_ ~ elevation + slope + tri + trees + grassland + shrubs,
          data = second, family = binomial(), weights = w)

data.frame(
  term = names(coef(f3))[-1],
  third_order  = round(coef(f3)[-1], 3),
  second_order = round(coef(f2)[-1], 3)
)

#> trees         trees      -0.045        0.381
#> grassland grassland      -0.477        0.224

Your turn
4a. Do any coefficients change sign or magnitude substantially? 4b. Which analysis is “right”?






NoteSolution






cmp <- data.frame(term = names(coef(f3))[-1],
                  third = coef(f3)[-1], second = coef(f2)[-1])

plot(cmp$third, cmp$second, pch = 16, col = "#1f6f78", cex = 1.4,
     xlab = "Third order (within own MCP)",
     ylab = "Second order (within population range)",
     main = "The domain changes the answer")
abline(0, 1, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 3)
text(cmp$third, cmp$second, cmp$term, pos = 3, cex = 0.65)







Points off the dashed 1:1 line are covariates whose apparent importance depends on the domain; points in the upper-left or lower-right quadrants have changed sign between the two analyses.
Neither is “right”. They answer different questions:


Second order — given the whole area the population occupies, where does Cilla place her range?

Third order — given the range she has already established, where within it does she go?

A covariate can drive the first decision and be irrelevant to the second, or act in opposite directions at the two scales — an animal may settle in a grass-rich part of the park and then, within it, seek out the scarce shade.
The obligation on you is to state the order and the availability domain explicitly, in the abstract, not buried in the methods. A habitat-selection result without that information cannot be interpreted.






ImportantThis also resolves an apparent contradiction with Class 5



In Class 5 we compared used points against points drawn from the convex hull of all six animals and found buffalo used grassland about 1.6× more than it was available — apparent selection.
Here, within Cilla’s own MCP, the grassland coefficient is negative.
Both are correct, and together they tell a coherent story: buffalo place their ranges in the grassy parts of the landscape (a second-order preference), and then, within a range that is already overwhelmingly grassland, they move towards the scarcer other things it contains.
The availability domain for Cilla is 309 km²; for the population it is 2,939 km² — nearly ten times larger, and a very different menu. Reporting the third-order coefficient as “buffalo avoid grassland” would be a serious misreading.

Task 5 — All six animals, two-stage

fit_one <- function(animal) {
  a <- trk |> filter(id == animal)
  dd <- a |>
    random_points(n = nrow(a) * 10) |>

           w = ifelse(case_, 1, 5000))

           data = dd, family = binomial(), weights = w)

}

Your turn
5a. Summarise across individuals: mean coefficient, SE, and a t-test against zero. 5b. Are the animals consistent?






NoteSolution






pop_level <- per_animal |>
  group_by(term) |>
  summarise(
    mean_beta = mean(beta),
    se        = sd(beta) / sqrt(n()),
    t         = mean_beta / se,
    p         = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n() - 1),
    n_positive = sum(beta > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_beta, se, t), \(z) round(z, 3)), p = round(p, 4)) |>

pop_level

#>   term      mean_beta    se      t      p n_positive
#>   <chr>         <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>      <int>
#> 1 grassland    -0.541 0.184 -2.94  0.0322          1
#> 2 tri          -0.394 0.213 -1.85  0.123           0
#> 3 shrubs       -0.37  0.213 -1.73  0.143           1
#> 4 trees        -0.103 0.112 -0.919 0.400           2

#> 6 slope         0.072 0.127  0.568 0.594           4


boxplot(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        las = 2, xlab = "", ylab = "Coefficient (per 1 SD)",
        main = "Individual coefficients, 6 buffalo")
abline(h = 0, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
stripchart(beta ~ term, data = per_animal, vertical = TRUE, add = TRUE,
           pch = 16, col = adjustcolor("black", 0.6), cex = 0.8)







This is the two-stage approach: each animal is one observation, so the degrees of freedom reflect the number of animals (6), not the number of points (hundreds of thousands). That is the honest accounting, and it is why the p-values here are far less impressive than those in Task 2 — as they should be.
The n_positive column is worth as much as the p-value: a covariate with the same sign in 6 of 6 animals is a consistent effect even if the mean is imprecise, while one that is positive in 3 and negative in 3 is not a population-level effect however tight the pooled interval looks.
With more animals you would move to a mixed model with random slopes (Muff et al. 2020). A random intercept alone is not enough — it lets individuals differ in overall intensity of use but forces them to share one selection coefficient, which badly under-states the uncertainty.

text:
Task 6 — Map the prediction

# Rebuild the covariate stack standardised the same way as the fitting data
cilla_mcp <- hr_isopleths(hr_mcp(cilla, levels = 0.99))
covs_crop <- crop(covs, vect(cilla_mcp)) |> mask(vect(cilla_mcp))

mu <- sapply(covars, \(v) mean(values(covs_crop[[v]]), na.rm = TRUE))
sdv <- sapply(covars, \(v) sd(values(covs_crop[[v]]), na.rm = TRUE))

z <- rast(covs_crop[[covars]])
for (v in covars) z[[v]] <- (covs_crop[[v]] - mu[v]) / sdv[v]

b <- coef(fit)
lin <- b[["elevation"]] * z[["elevation"]] +
       b[["slope"]]     * z[["slope"]] +
       b[["tri"]]       * z[["tri"]] +
       b[["trees"]]     * z[["trees"]] +
       b[["grassland"]] * z[["grassland"]] +
       b[["shrubs"]]    * z[["shrubs"]]

rsf_map <- exp(lin)
names(rsf_map) <- "rsf"

plot(rsf_map, col = hcl.colors(50, "Viridis"),
     main = "Predicted relative selection — Cilla")
points(cilla$x_, cilla$y_, pch = 16, cex = 0.15,
       col = adjustcolor("white", 0.4))













NoteWhy the legend has no units





The values are relative, proportional to the probability of use by an unknown constant. A cell with value 4 is predicted to be used about twice as intensively as a cell with value 2 — but neither is a probability.
It is standard practice to rescale the surface to 0–1, or to bin it into ordered quantiles, purely for display. Do not let that rescaling tempt you into calling it a probability of occurrence.
Note also that the map is only meaningful inside the availability domain. Extrapolating an RSF beyond the range of covariate values the animal actually encountered is unsupported — the model has no information there.

title: Exercise 7 — Fitting a resource selection function
text:
Self-check

You double the number of available points and your p-values all become smaller. What does this tell you about your covariates?

They are more important than you thought
Nothing — you increased the precision of your description of availability, not of your observations of the animal
The model is now overfitted
The weights were wrong


Available points are a description of the landscape, which you can sample as finely as your computer allows. Drawing more of them sharpens your estimate of what was on offer, so the standard errors fall — but you have not observed the animal any more closely, and no new biological information has entered the model.
This is why p-values are near-meaningless in used–available designs. What you should report: effect sizes as exp(beta) on standardised covariates, confidence intervals, consistency across individuals, and out-of-sample validation.
It is also why the two-stage approach in Task 5 is so useful: it makes the degrees of freedom reflect the number of animals, which is the sample size you actually have.



In Class 5 you found grassland covers 56% of the broader availability domain but 90% of used points, and concluded buffalo select grassland. A colleague objects that grassland is the commonest habitat there. Is your conclusion consistent?

Yes — used exceeds available, which is exactly what selection means
No — you cannot select for the commonest habitat
Only if the sample sizes are equal
Cannot say without the p-value


Selection is use relative to availability, so a habitat can be both common and selected. 90% use against 56% availability is a ratio of about 1.6 — real selection, and it matches the used/available table you computed in Class 5.
The common confusion runs the other way: an animal found mostly in the dominant habitat is often described as “preferring” it when the use/availability ratio is 1 or below. That is why raw use frequencies are never enough, and why the availability sample is not optional.

Your turn
2a. Describe the two states in words. 2b. What is the expected dwell time in each?






NoteSolution






round(m2$mle$stepPar, 3)
#>           state 1 state 2
#> mean       15.329 344.272
#> sd         12.810 327.737

round(m2$mle$anglePar, 3)

#> mean            3.078  -0.019

State 1 — mean step of about 15 m with very low angular concentration and a mean turning angle near π: the animal barely moves and reverses direction constantly. This is an encamped state: resting, ruminating, or grazing within a very small patch.
State 2 — mean step of a few hundred metres, mean turning angle near 0 and higher concentration: directed movement.
Dwell times: roughly 2 hours in the encamped state and about 8 hours in the moving state. Note that these are in hours only because the data are hourly — the units of a dwell time are always “number of sampling intervals”.

states <- viterbi(m2)
round(table(states) / length(states), 3)
#> states
#>     1     2 
#> 0.215 0.785







Warning



The model has given you state 1 and state 2. Calling them “resting” and “travelling” is an interpretation, and everything above is consistent with several other stories. To make the labels a measurement rather than a guess you would need external evidence: accelerometer data, direct observation, or known activity patterns.

title: Exercise 6 — Fitting a hidden Markov model
text:
Task 4 — How many states?

m3 <- fitHMM(
  pd, nbStates = 3,
  stepPar0  = c(30, 200, 800, 30, 200, 800, 0.01, 0.001, 0.001),
  anglePar0 = c(0, 0, 0, 0.5, 1, 3)
)

data.frame(states = c(2, 3), AIC = c(AIC(m2), AIC(m3)))
#>   states      AIC
#> 1      2 151969.4
#> 2      3 150777.9
round(m3$mle$stepPar, 1)
#>           state 1 state 2 state 3
#> mean         17.1   187.3   569.1
#> sd           14.9   138.5   398.7
#> zero-mass     0.0     0.0     0.0

Your turn
4a. AIC prefers 3 states. Should you report 3 states? 4b. What would make you confident that a third state is real?






NoteSolution






round(m3$mle$anglePar, 2)
#>               state 1 state 2 state 3
#> mean             3.06     0.0   -0.05
#> concentration    0.20     0.9    0.66
round(1 / (1 - diag(m3$mle$gamma)), 2)
#> [1] 2.12 3.02 3.40
round(table(viterbi(m3)) / nrow(pd), 3)
#> 
#>     1     2     3 
#> 0.253 0.415 0.332

AIC is lower for 3 states, and it would very likely keep falling for 4 and 5. That is what mixture models do: extra components always improve the fit to the shape of the data, whether or not they correspond to behaviours.
Ask instead:


Are the states distinct? If two states have overlapping step-length distributions and similar turning angles, the model has split one behaviour in two.

Are the dwell times plausible? A state occupied for a single step at a time is a statistical artefact, not a behaviour.

Is any state rare? A state holding 2% of steps is usually absorbing outliers.

Does it survive? Refit on a different individual, or a different season. A real behaviour recurs; an artefact does not.

Here the third state sits between the other two, which is biologically reasonable for a large grazer (rest / graze / travel) — but you should say that you chose 3 for that reason, not because AIC said so.
Report the simplest model that answers your question and passes its checks, and state your criterion in the methods.

Task 5 — Check the residuals

pr <- pseudoRes(m2)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
qqnorm(pr$stepRes, main = "Step pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4))
qqline(pr$stepRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
qqnorm(pr$angleRes, main = "Angle pseudo-residuals", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
       col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.4))
qqline(pr$angleRes, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







NoteReading a pseudo-residual plot





If the model describes the data, pseudo-residuals are standard normal and the points lie on the line. Departures tell you where the model fails:


Heavy tails — the step-length distribution is wrong (try log-normal or Weibull), or outliers remain

Systematic curvature — the wrong number of states, or a state whose distribution family does not match

Structure when plotted against time — a covariate is missing: perhaps behaviour depends on time of day and you have not let it

This is the HMM equivalent of plotting residuals in a regression, and it is skipped in far too many papers.

Task 6 — A different kind of segmentation
Leo the vulture needs change-point thinking, not state classification. The question is when did migration start, and the NSD profile from Class 4 is enough to answer it.

vul <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |> distinct(t, .keep_all = TRUE) |> arrange(t)

vt <- make_track(vul, x, y, t, crs = 4326) |> transform_coords(crs_to = 6933)

daily <- vt |>
  mutate(day = as.Date(t_)) |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(x = mean(x_), y = mean(y_), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(day) |>
  mutate(disp_km = c(NA, sqrt(diff(x)^2 + diff(y)^2)) / 1000)

daily <- daily |> mutate(migrating = disp_km > 50)

plot(daily$day, daily$disp_km, type = "h",
     col = ifelse(daily$migrating, "#c1440e", "grey65"),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Daily displacement (km)",
     main = "Leo: daily displacement, migration days in red")
abline(h = 50, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)







Your turn
6a. How many migration days per year, and in which months? 6b. Why is a simple threshold acceptable here, when it would not be for the buffalo?






NoteSolution






daily |>
  filter(migrating) |>
  count(year = year(day), name = "migration_days")
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>    year migration_days
#>   <dbl>          <int>
#> 1  2007             57
#> 2  2008             85
#> 3  2009             80
#> 4  2010             67
#> 5  2011             40
#> 6  2012             13
#> 7  2013              5

daily |>
  filter(migrating) |>
  count(month = month(day, label = TRUE), name = "days")
#> # A tibble: 9 × 2
#>   month  days
#>   <ord> <int>
#> 1 Jan       6
#> 2 Feb       6
#> 3 Mar      47
#> 4 Apr      84
#> 5 May       5
#> 6 Sep      12
#> 7 Oct     109
#> 8 Nov      66
#> 9 Dec      12

Migration days cluster strongly in the spring and autumn months, exactly as the NSD sawtooth in Class 4 suggested.
Why a threshold is defensible here. The two behaviours are separated by roughly an order of magnitude: a resident vulture moves a few kilometres a day, a migrating one moves hundreds. The distribution of daily displacement is clearly bimodal with a wide, empty valley between the modes, so the exact threshold barely matters.

hist(log10(daily$disp_km + 1), breaks = 50, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     xlab = "log10(daily displacement km + 1)", main = "Two clearly separated modes")
abline(v = log10(51), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)







For the buffalo there is no such valley: resting, grazing and travelling produce overlapping step-length distributions with no gap to cut at. That is precisely when you need a model that assigns states probabilistically and uses the time dependence to resolve the overlap — an HMM.
The general rule: if a histogram of your metric shows a clean gap, a threshold is honest and transparent. If it does not, a threshold is an arbitrary decision dressed as a result.

title: Exercise 6 — Fitting a hidden Markov model
text:
Self-check

Your 2-state HMM assigns 97% of steps to state 1 and 3% to state 2, and state 2 has a mean step length of 12 km. What has probably happened?

The animal genuinely travels 3% of the time
State 2 is absorbing location errors rather than describing a behaviour
The model needs more states
The sampling interval is too short


A rare state with an extreme mean is the classic signature of a model mopping up outliers. Twelve kilometres in one step is implausible for most terrestrial mammals at an hourly interval, and the HMM has done what it was asked to do: found the mixture that best fits the data, including the bad points.
Clean first, then model. Find the offending steps, look at them on a map, decide whether they are real, and remove them (or the affected bursts) before refitting. This is why Task 1 drops the 63 km steps.
More states would not help — you would simply get more outlier-absorbing states.



You want to know whether buffalo are more likely to start moving when it is hot. What do you change in fitHMM()?

Add temperature to stepPar0
Pass formula = ~ temperature so the covariate acts on the transition probabilities
Fit separate models for hot and cold days
Nothing — HMMs cannot include covariates


The question is about switching between behaviours, and switching is governed by the transition probability matrix. formula = ~ temperature makes the transition probabilities a (multinomial-logit) function of temperature, which is exactly the hypothesis.
Putting a covariate on the state-dependent distributions instead would ask a different question — “does the animal travel faster when it is hot”, given that it is already travelling.
Fitting separate models for hot and cold days throws away the transitions between them and gives you no test of the difference.
This is where Class 5 and Class 6 join up: annotate each fix with the contemporaneous covariate, then let it drive the transitions.

#>                mean
#> grassland 0.4007486

Same CRS, same resolution — and extents that agree to within floating-point noise: lc reports 31.3999999999942 where elev reports 31.4. terra tolerates a discrepancy that small and stacks them happily, which is why c(elev, lc) works in Task 2.
Do not rely on that. In real work rasters come from different providers on genuinely different grids, and you must align them explicitly — project() to a common CRS, then resample() one onto the other’s grid. Always align before stacking, never after.

Task 2 — Derived terrain covariates
Raw elevation is rarely the thing an animal responds to. Slope and ruggedness usually are.

terr <- terrain(elev, v = c("slope", "TRI"), unit = "degrees")
names(terr) <- c("slope", "tri")

covs <- c(elev, terr, lc)
names(covs)
#> [1] "elevation" "slope"     "tri"       "trees"     "grassland" "shrubs"   
#> [7] "cropland"


plot(terr, col = hcl.colors(50, "Inferno"), nc = 2)













Tip



TRI (terrain ruggedness index) is the mean absolute difference between a cell and its neighbours. For animals it often matters more than slope: a uniformly steep hillside is easy to traverse, a broken one is not.

Task 3 — Annotate the track

clean <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(id = individual.local.identifier,
            t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x  = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)

trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326)

used <- trk |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326) |>
  bind_cols(terra::extract(covs, vect(
    st_as_sf(trk, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326)
  ))[, -1])

summary(used[, c("elevation", "slope", "trees", "grassland")] |> st_drop_geometry())
#>    elevation         slope             trees           grassland     
#>  Min.   :148.0   Min.   :0.03109   Min.   :0.00000   Min.   :0.0000  
#>  1st Qu.:239.0   1st Qu.:0.35321   1st Qu.:0.00000   1st Qu.:0.8622  
#>  Median :265.0   Median :0.47231   Median :0.00040   Median :0.9624  
#>  Mean   :260.5   Mean   :0.60465   Mean   :0.02831   Mean   :0.9000  
#>  3rd Qu.:287.0   3rd Qu.:0.62735   3rd Qu.:0.03440   3rd Qu.:0.9956  
#>  Max.   :422.0   Max.   :5.41180   Max.   :0.86910   Max.   :1.0000  
#>  NAs    :1       NAs    :1

Your turn
3a. Now generate available points across the study area and annotate them too. 3b. Compare used vs available for each covariate. What stands out?






NoteSolution






set.seed(1)

# Available = random points within the buffalo's collective range
hull <- st_convex_hull(st_union(used))
avail_pts <- st_sample(hull, size = nrow(used), type = "random")

avail <- st_sf(geometry = avail_pts) |>
  bind_cols(terra::extract(covs, vect(st_sf(geometry = avail_pts)))[, -1])

comp <- bind_rows(
  used  |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(elevation, slope, tri, trees, grassland, shrubs) |> mutate(what = "used"),
  avail |> st_drop_geometry() |> select(elevation, slope, tri, trees, grassland, shrubs) |> mutate(what = "available")
)

comp |>
  pivot_longer(-what) |>
  group_by(name, what) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(value, na.rm = TRUE), 3), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = what, values_from = mean) |>
  mutate(ratio = round(used / available, 2))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   name      available    used ratio
#>   <chr>         <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 elevation   280.    260.     0.93
#> 2 grassland     0.561   0.9    1.6 
#> 3 shrubs        0.316   0.05   0.16
#> 4 slope         0.662   0.605  0.91
#> 5 trees         0.114   0.028  0.25
#> 6 tri          10.4     9.33   0.9


par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in c("elevation", "slope", "tri", "trees", "grassland", "shrubs")) {
  d_u <- density(comp[[v]][comp$what == "used"], na.rm = TRUE)
  d_a <- density(comp[[v]][comp$what == "available"], na.rm = TRUE)
  plot(d_a, col = "grey50", lwd = 2, main = v, xlab = "",
       ylim = c(0, max(d_u$y, d_a$y)))
  lines(d_u, col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2)
  if (v == "elevation") {
    legend("topright", c("available", "used"), col = c("grey50", "#1f6f78"),
           lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
  }
}






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Where the teal (used) curve sits to the right of the grey (available) curve, the animals are using more of that covariate than the landscape offers — selection. To the left is avoidance.
This side-by-side comparison of used and available distributions is the idea behind a resource selection function. Class 7 turns it into a model that handles several covariates at once and gives you uncertainty.

title: Exercise 5 — Environmental annotation
text:
Task 4 — Point or buffer?
The scale at which you measure the environment is a hypothesis about how far the animal can perceive. Let us ask for tree cover averaged over a neighbourhood.

pts <- st_as_sf(trk, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 4326) |> vect()

at_point <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts)[, 2]
buf_500  <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts, buffer = 500,  fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
buf_2000 <- terra::extract(covs[["trees"]], pts, buffer = 2000, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]

data.frame(
  scale = c("at fix", "buffer = 500", "buffer = 2000"),
  mean  = round(c(mean(at_point,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  mean(buf_500,   na.rm = TRUE),
                  mean(buf_2000,  na.rm = TRUE)), 4),
  sd    = round(c(sd(at_point, na.rm = TRUE),
                  sd(buf_500,  na.rm = TRUE),
                  sd(buf_2000, na.rm = TRUE)), 4)
)
#>           scale   mean     sd
#> 1        at fix 0.0283 0.0553
#> 2  buffer = 500 0.0283 0.0553
#> 3 buffer = 2000 0.0283 0.0553

identical(at_point, buf_500)
#> [1] TRUE
identical(at_point, buf_2000)
#> [1] TRUE







ImportantThe buffer= argument was silently ignored



All three columns are identical. In this version of terra (1.9.27), passing buffer= to extract() with point geometries does nothing at all — no error, no warning, just the at-point values three times over.
Had you not checked, you would have reported a “multi-scale analysis” in which every scale was the same scale.
The habit: when an argument is supposed to change the answer, verify that it did. identical() costs one line.


The reliable way is to build the buffer polygons yourself. Work in a projected CRS so the radius is honestly in metres.

covs_utm <- project(covs, "EPSG:32736")
pts_utm  <- project(pts, "EPSG:32736")

buffer_mean <- function(r, p, width) {
  terra::extract(r, buffer(p, width = width), fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE)[, 2]
}

scales <- c(500, 2000, 5000)
tab <- lapply(scales, function(w) {
  v <- buffer_mean(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm, w)
  data.frame(radius_m = w, mean = mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(v, na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows()

at_pt <- terra::extract(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm)[, 2]

bind_rows(
  data.frame(radius_m = 0, mean = mean(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE), sd = sd(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE)),
  tab
) |> mutate(across(c(mean, sd), \(z) round(z, 4)))
#>   radius_m   mean     sd
#> 1        0 0.0280 0.0468
#> 2      500 0.0279 0.0455
#> 3     2000 0.0276 0.0342
#> 4     5000 0.0274 0.0313

Your turn
4a. What happens to the variance as the radius grows? 4b. Why does a 500 m radius barely differ from the point value? 4c. Which scale would you choose, and on what grounds?






NoteSolution






b2000 <- buffer_mean(covs_utm[["trees"]], pts_utm, 2000)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(at_pt, b2000, pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.2),
     xlab = "Tree cover at the fix", ylab = "Mean within 2 km",
     main = "The same covariate at two scales")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)

plot(c(0, scales), c(sd(at_pt, na.rm = TRUE), tab$sd), type = "b", pch = 16,
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2, xlab = "Buffer radius (m)",
     ylab = "SD of the covariate", main = "Smoothing destroys contrast")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Variance falls as the radius grows: you are averaging over more cells, so extremes cancel. The mean barely moves; the spread collapses.
That has a direct statistical consequence. A smoothed covariate has less contrast between used and available points, so the effect size you can detect shrinks, and a real preference can be smoothed into non-significance.
Why 500 m does almost nothing. The raster cells are 30 arc-seconds — about 900 m on the ground here:

round(res(covs_utm))
#> [1] 893 893

A 500 m radius fits inside a single cell, so the “neighbourhood mean” is mostly that one cell’s value. A buffer smaller than your pixel is not a scale — it is a rounding error. If you want a genuine multi-scale analysis, your radii must be several times the cell size, or you need finer data.
How to choose. From biology, before you look at the results: how far can this animal see, smell, or remember? For buffalo in savanna, a few hundred metres to a couple of kilometres is defensible. What you must not do is fit the model at ten radii and report the one with the smallest p-value — that is a garden of forking paths, and the “optimal scale” it finds will not replicate.
If scale genuinely is your question, there are principled multi-scale approaches — but you have to say so in advance.

title: Exercise 5 — Environmental annotation
text:
Task 5 — Time-matched annotation
Static covariates are easy. Now the one that actually matters.

prec <- rast("data/kruger_prec_monthly.tif")
nlyr(prec)
#> [1] 12
names(prec)
#>  [1] "prec_01" "prec_02" "prec_03" "prec_04" "prec_05" "prec_06" "prec_07"
#>  [8] "prec_08" "prec_09" "prec_10" "prec_11" "prec_12"

Twelve layers: the long-term average precipitation for each calendar month. Kruger has a strong wet/dry seasonality, so this is a real seasonal signal.

plot(prec[[c(1, 4, 7, 10)]], col = hcl.colors(50, "Blues", rev = TRUE), nc = 2)







The naive approach — one layer for everything:

static <- terra::extract(prec[[1]], pts)[, 2]   # January, for all fixes
summary(static)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    94.0    97.0   102.0   103.5   111.0   116.0

The correct approach — each fix gets the layer for its own month:

month_idx <- as.integer(format(trk$t_, "%m"))

all_months <- terra::extract(prec, pts)[, -1]   # one column per month
matched <- all_months[cbind(seq_len(nrow(all_months)), month_idx)]

summary(matched)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    5.00   19.00   33.00   45.44   72.00  105.00







ImportantThe indexing trick



all_months[cbind(row, col)] is matrix indexing: it picks element [row_i, col_i] for each i. That single line is the whole of time-matched annotation. For a real NDVI time series you would build col with findInterval() against the layer dates instead of format(t, "%m").


Your turn
5a. How different are the static and time-matched values? 5b. Do the buffalo experience more or less rain than the landscape average?






NoteSolution






cmp <- data.frame(static = static, matched = matched)
round(cor(cmp, use = "complete.obs"), 3)
#>         static matched
#> static   1.000  -0.417
#> matched -0.417   1.000

cmp |>
  summarise(mean_static = round(mean(static, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_matched = round(mean(matched, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_abs_diff = round(mean(abs(static - matched), na.rm = TRUE), 1))
#>   mean_static mean_matched mean_abs_diff
#> 1       103.5         45.4            58


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(static, matched, pch = 16, cex = 0.2, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.2),
     xlab = "January value (static)", ylab = "Value for the fix's own month",
     main = "Static vs time-matched")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)

boxplot(matched ~ month_idx, col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        xlab = "Month", ylab = "Precipitation (mm)",
        main = "What the animals actually experienced")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

The two are barely related. The static version varies only in space; the matched version varies in space and time, and the temporal swing here dominates — Kruger’s wet season delivers an order of magnitude more rain than its dry season.
Any model using the static column would be answering “do buffalo prefer places that are wet in January”, not “do buffalo respond to rainfall”. Those are different questions, and they can easily give opposite answers.






Note



These are long-term monthly climatologies, not the actual weather of 2005–2006. They carry the seasonal cycle but not the year-to-year anomaly. For real work you would use a dated product — MODIS NDVI composites, ERA5 reanalysis, or Movebank’s Env-DATA — and match on the actual date with findInterval(). The mechanics are identical; only the layer dates change.

title: Exercise 5 — Environmental annotation
text:
Self-check

You extract NDVI with terra::extract() and summary() reports a range of −2000 to 9500. What is wrong?

The raster is corrupt
You have raw stored integers — apply the scale factor, and handle the fill value
NDVI can legitimately take these values
The CRS is wrong


NDVI is bounded by −1 and +1 by definition — it is a normalised difference. Values in the thousands mean the product stores NDVI as scaled integers to save space; MODIS uses a scale factor of 0.0001, so 9500 → 0.95.
The negative extreme is usually the fill value for missing data (MODIS uses −3000), which must be set to NA, not multiplied. Leave it in and it becomes a strongly negative NDVI at exactly the cloudy pixels where you had no data.
Rule: after every extraction, summary() the new column and ask whether the range is physically possible.



Your study area straddles a national border and you stack a land-cover raster from one country with a DEM from another. c(dem, lc) throws an error about extents. What is the right fix?

Crop both to their intersection and hope the grids align
project() to a common CRS if needed, then resample() one onto the other’s grid
Convert both to data frames and join by coordinates
Use extract() separately on each and skip stacking


Stacking requires identical CRS, extent and cell alignment. Cropping alone fixes the extent but not the alignment — two 30 m grids offset by 7 m are still incompatible.
resample() interpolates one raster onto the other’s grid. Use method = "near" for categorical data such as land-cover classes, or you will invent classes that do not exist.
Extracting separately does work and avoids the problem, but only if you never need the layers in a single object.

title: Exercise 4 — Steps, angles, displacement and home range
text:
Task 1 — Steps, angles and speeds

st <- trk_hr |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, steps_by_burst)) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

st <- st |> mutate(speed_kmh = (sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(dt_, units = "hours"))

st |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            median_sl = round(median(sl_)),
            q99_sl = round(quantile(sl_, 0.99)),
            max_sl = round(max(sl_)))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>       n median_sl q99_sl max_sl
#>   <int>     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 22588       152   1948  63103

Your turn
1a. Plot the distribution of step lengths and of turning angles. 1b. What does the turning-angle distribution tell you?






NoteSolution






par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

hist(st$sl_[st$sl_ < 3000], breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Step length (< 3 km)", xlab = "metres")

hist(st$ta_, breaks = 40, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Turning angle", xlab = "radians")

# A rose diagram respects the circular nature of the data
ta <- st$ta_[!is.na(st$ta_)]
brk <- seq(-pi, pi, length.out = 25)
cnt <- table(cut(ta, brk))
mid <- (head(brk, -1) + tail(brk, -1)) / 2
plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1), asp = 1,
     axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = "Turning angles (rose)")
r <- as.numeric(cnt) / max(cnt)
for (i in seq_along(mid)) {
  lines(c(0, r[i] * cos(mid[i])), c(0, r[i] * sin(mid[i])),
        col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 6)
}






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Step lengths are strongly right-skewed: most steps are short (the animal is resting or grazing), with a long tail of directed movement. This is why step lengths are modelled with a gamma or exponential distribution, never a normal one.
Turning angles peak sharply at 0 and again — more weakly — near ±π. The peak at 0 is directional persistence: an animal that was heading somewhere tends to keep heading there. The bumps near ±π are reversals, typically an animal turning back within a patch, plus some GPS error at very short steps.
A uniform turning-angle distribution would mean no directional memory at all — a simple random walk. Real animals are never that.

title: Exercise 4 — Steps, angles, displacement and home range
text:
Task 2 — Scale dependence, demonstrated
Resample the same animals at four intervals and compare.
For turning angles we need a circular summary. The standard one is the mean resultant length \(\rho = \overline{\cos\theta}\): it is 1 for perfectly straight movement and 0 for a uniform (memoryless) distribution.

rates <- list(`1 h` = hours(1), `3 h` = hours(3),
              `6 h` = hours(6), `12 h` = hours(12))

scale_tab <- lapply(names(rates), function(nm) {
  tr <- resample_by_id(trk, rates[[nm]], minutes(15))
  s <- tr |> nest(data = -id) |>
    mutate(data = lapply(data, steps_by_burst)) |> unnest(cols = data)
  ta <- s$ta_[!is.na(s$ta_)]
  data.frame(rate = nm, n_steps = nrow(s),
             median_sl_m = round(median(s$sl_)),
             rho = round(mean(cos(ta)), 3),
             frac_straight = round(mean(abs(ta) < pi / 4), 3))
}) |> bind_rows()

scale_tab
#>   rate n_steps median_sl_m   rho frac_straight
#> 1  1 h   22596         152 0.258         0.416
#> 2  3 h    7567         472 0.294         0.423
#> 3  6 h    4002         887 0.223         0.393
#> 4 12 h    2011        1500 0.048         0.290

For reference, a memoryless walk would give rho = 0 and frac_straight = 0.25.
Your turn
2a. What happens to median step length as the interval grows? 2b. What happens to directional persistence — and is it monotonic?






NoteSolution





Step length increases, from ~150 m at 1 h to ~1.5 km at 12 h — but far less than proportionally. Twelve times the interval buys only about ten times the displacement, because the path doubles back on itself. If movement were perfectly directed the relationship would be linear; the shortfall is the tortuosity.
Directional persistence collapses, but not smoothly:

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
barplot(scale_tab$median_sl_m, names.arg = scale_tab$rate, col = "#1f6f78",
        border = "white", ylab = "Median step length (m)",
        xlab = "Sampling interval", main = "Step length grows with interval")
barplot(scale_tab$rho, names.arg = scale_tab$rate, col = "#b8860b",
        border = "white", ylab = expression(rho == bar(cos(theta))),
        xlab = "Sampling interval", main = "Persistence collapses by 12 h")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Persistence holds up to about 6 hours and has essentially vanished at 12 hours (\(\rho \approx 0.05\), frac_straight ≈ 0.29 against the uniform 0.25). So for these buffalo the timescale of directional memory sits somewhere between 6 and 12 hours.
The non-monotonic bit is the interesting part. \(\rho\) is lower at 1 h than at 3 h. That is not biology — it is measurement. At an hourly interval many steps are only a few tens of metres (a resting or grazing animal), and when the step is comparable to the GPS error the direction of that step is largely noise. Randomised directions drag \(\rho\) down.
Two practical consequences:

A correlated random walk fitted at 12 h would report almost no correlation, and you would wrongly conclude the animal moves at random.
At very fine intervals, turning angles are contaminated by positional error. This is why step-selection analyses (Class 8) are usually run at an interval where typical step length comfortably exceeds GPS error.

Task 3 — Net squared displacement

nsd_of <- function(d) {
  d <- d[order(d$t_), ]
  data.frame(t = d$t_, nsd = (d$x_ - d$x_[1])^2 + (d$y_ - d$y_[1])^2)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

cil <- nsd_of(trk_hr[trk_hr$id == "Cilla", ])
plot(cil$t, cil$nsd / 1e6, type = "l", col = "#1f6f78",
     xlab = "", ylab = "NSD (km²)", main = "Buffalo 'Cilla' — sedentary")

vul <- read.csv("data/vulture_leo.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(t = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
            x = location.long, y = location.lat) |>
  filter(!is.na(x)) |> distinct(t, .keep_all = TRUE) |> arrange(t)
vt <- make_track(vul, x, y, t, crs = 4326) |> transform_coords(crs_to = 6933)
v <- nsd_of(vt)
plot(v$t, v$nsd / 1e6, type = "l", col = "#c1440e",
     xlab = "", ylab = "NSD (km²)", main = "Vulture 'Leo' — migratory")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))







NoteReading these two plots





Cilla rises quickly to a ceiling and stays there, oscillating. That is the signature of a sedentary animal with a bounded home range: once it has explored its range, it cannot get further from the start.
Leo shows six clean cycles: a sigmoid rise (autumn migration), a plateau (wintering), a sigmoid fall (spring migration), a plateau (breeding). This is the textbook migratory NSD profile.
Note the CRS: Leo spans 47° of latitude, so no UTM zone works. EPSG:6933 is a global equal-area projection — appropriate for continental-scale distances and areas.
NSD is a one-line diagnostic and it should be the first plot you make for any new track. It tells you immediately whether a home range is a meaningful thing to estimate.

     main = "Buffalo 'Cilla': MCP (grey) vs KDE (teal)")

points(cilla$x_, cilla$y_, pch = 16, cex = 0.2,
       col = adjustcolor("black", 0.25))







Your turn
4a. Which is larger, and why? 4b. What does the 50% contour represent?






NoteSolution





The MCP is convex by construction, so it swallows any concavity in the animal’s actual use — here, areas it moved around rather than through. The KDE can be concave and can even be disjoint, so it hugs the used area more tightly.
The 50% contour is conventionally called the core area: the smallest region containing half the probability mass of the utilisation distribution. It is a convention, not a biological threshold — but it is far more informative than the 95% boundary, because it shows where the animal actually concentrates.

bind_rows(
  hr_area(mcp95) |> mutate(method = "MCP"),
  hr_area(kde95) |> mutate(method = "KDE")
) |>
  transmute(method, level, area_km2 = round(area / 1e6, 1)) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = method, values_from = area_km2)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   level   MCP   KDE
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0.95 264.  292. 
#> 2  0.5   75.5  61.2

text:
Task 5 — Show yourself the autocorrelation problem
If KDE assumed independence and our fixes are autocorrelated, then thinning the data should change the answer systematically. Let us check.

thin_every <- function(tr, k) tr[seq(1, nrow(tr), by = k), ]

thin_tab <- lapply(c(1, 2, 6, 12, 24, 48), function(k) {
  d <- thin_every(cilla, k)
  if (nrow(d) < 30) return(NULL)
  a <- hr_area(hr_kde(d, levels = 0.95))
  data.frame(every = paste0(k, " h"), n = nrow(d),
             kde95_km2 = round(a$area / 1e6, 1))
}) |> bind_rows()

thin_tab
#>   every    n kde95_km2
#> 1   1 h 3518     292.2
#> 2   2 h 1759     303.6
#> 3   6 h  587     330.8
#> 4  12 h  294     345.2
#> 5  24 h  147     378.9
#> 6  48 h   74     400.2

Your turn
5a. What happens to the KDE area as you thin? 5b. What would happen if the fixes were genuinely independent?






NoteSolution






plot(thin_tab$n, thin_tab$kde95_km2, type = "b", pch = 16, log = "x",
     col = "#1f6f78", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Number of fixes (log)", ylab = "95% KDE area (km²)",
     main = "KDE area depends on how many fixes you kept")







The estimate is not stable — and it drifts in a consistent direction. The 95% KDE area grows steadily as we thin, from roughly 290 km² at hourly sampling to about 400 km² at 48-hourly, a ~37% difference for the same animal over the same period.
If the fixes were independent draws from a fixed utilisation distribution, the KDE area would converge to a constant as \(n\) grows — more data, less noise, same answer. Instead the denser data give systematically smaller ranges, because adding more autocorrelated fixes adds almost no new information about the utilisation distribution while the bandwidth selector behaves as though it does. The effective sample size is far smaller than n.
This is precisely the problem AKDE was built to solve — and precisely why a 95% KDE from 8,000 hourly fixes is not comparable to one from 60 VHF fixes.
