title: Exercise 4 — Steps, angles, displacement and home range
text:
Task 6 — AKDE with ctmm

ctmm fits a continuous-time movement model first, then uses its autocorrelation structure to weight the kernel estimate.






Warning



Model selection is genuinely slow — minutes, not seconds. We thin to 6-hourly fixes here so it finishes during class. For real work, use the full track and be patient.



library(ctmm)

cil6 <- thin_every(cilla, 6)

mb <- data.frame(
  timestamp = cil6$t_,
  location.long = NA, location.lat = NA,
  individual.local.identifier = "Cilla"
)
# ctmm wants geographic coordinates; convert the UTM track back
ll <- sf::st_coordinates(
  sf::st_transform(sf::st_as_sf(cil6, coords = c("x_", "y_"), crs = 32736), 4326)
)
mb$location.long <- ll[, 1]
mb$location.lat  <- ll[, 2]

tel <- as.telemetry(mb, timeformat = "auto")

guess <- ctmm.guess(tel, interactive = FALSE)
fit   <- ctmm.select(tel, guess, verbose = FALSE)

summary(fit)
#> $name
#> [1] "OUF anisotropic"
#> 
#> $DOF
#>      mean      area diffusion     speed 
#>  15.55335  26.82906 232.67046 163.80052 
#> 
#> $CI
#>                                          low        est       high
#> area (square kilometers)          257.316665 391.034715 552.287368
#> τ[position] (days)                  3.169814   4.953404   7.740585
#> τ[velocity] (hours)                 1.487567   1.919526   2.476918
#> speed (kilometers/day)              9.828279  10.643243  11.457383
#> diffusion (square kilometers/day)   7.402496   8.453952   9.574215


ak <- akde(tel, fit)
summary(ak)$CI
#>                               low      est     high
#> area (square kilometers) 230.5808 350.4051 494.9032

Your turn
6a. Compare the AKDE estimate with the KDE estimate on the same thinned data. 6b. What does the confidence interval tell you?






NoteSolution






kde_same <- hr_area(hr_kde(cil6, levels = 0.95))$area / 1e6
akde_ci  <- summary(ak, units = FALSE)$CI / 1e6   # m² → km²

c(KDE_km2 = round(kde_same, 1))
#> KDE_km2 
#>   330.8
round(akde_ci, 1)
#>                        low   est  high
#> area (square meters) 230.6 350.4 494.9

Two things to notice.
The point estimate differs. AKDE corrects for the autocorrelation that classical KDE ignores, and for this animal it typically comes out larger.
AKDE gives you a confidence interval, and it is wide. That width is the honest statement of how much your data actually constrain the answer. A single number from classical KDE hides exactly that uncertainty — which is why it is so easy to over-interpret small differences between individuals or between years.
The model summary is also worth reading: ctmm.select() chose a movement model (OU, OUF, IID…), and the “area” row of summary(fit) reports the range-residency estimate. If the selected model has no range residency, the animal is not exhibiting home-range behaviour and an AKDE area is not a meaningful quantity — the software will tell you, which classical KDE never does.

title: Exercise 4 — Steps, angles, displacement and home range
text:
Self-check

You resample a track from hourly to 6-hourly and the mean turning angle distribution becomes almost uniform. What does this tell you?

The animal’s behaviour changed
Directional persistence operates on a shorter timescale than 6 hours
The resampling introduced an error
Turning angles are always uniform at long intervals for all species


Directional persistence is a short-term property of movement. At a six-hour interval the animal has changed activity several times, so the direction of one step carries almost no information about the next, and turning angles approach uniform.
This is a statement about the timescale of the behaviour relative to your sampling, not about the animal changing. It also matters practically: a correlated random walk fitted at 6 hours will report almost no correlation, and you would wrongly conclude the animal moves at random.



ctmm.select() chooses an IID (independent, identically distributed) model for your track. What does that mean for your home-range analysis?

AKDE will be identical to KDE, so use whichever
The fixes carry no detectable autocorrelation — usually a sign your sampling is too sparse to resolve the movement process
The animal has no home range
The model failed to converge


An IID model says the data show no detectable correlation between successive positions. For a modern GPS track that is nearly always a symptom, not a finding: fixes so far apart in time that the movement process between them is unresolved.
In that regime AKDE reduces to something close to classical KDE — it has no autocorrelation to correct for. The estimate is not wrong, but you should say plainly that the sampling could not resolve the movement process, and be cautious comparing it with estimates from denser data.

title: Exercise 3 — Clean, resample and map a track
text:
Task 1 — Build a track

raw <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(
    id = individual.local.identifier,
    t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
    x  = location.long,
    y  = location.lat
  )

nrow(raw)
#> [1] 28410

Now clean, counting every step. This block is the template for every dataset you will ever handle.

n0 <- nrow(raw)

clean <- raw |> filter(!is.na(x), !is.na(y))
n1 <- nrow(clean)

clean <- clean |> filter(!(x == 0 & y == 0))
n2 <- nrow(clean)

clean <- clean |> distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE)
n3 <- nrow(clean)

data.frame(
  step = c("raw", "drop missing coords", "drop (0,0)", "drop duplicate id+time"),
  rows = c(n0, n1, n2, n3),
  removed = c(NA, n0 - n1, n1 - n2, n2 - n3)
)
#>                     step  rows removed
#> 1                    raw 28410      NA
#> 2    drop missing coords 28410       0
#> 3             drop (0,0) 28410       0
#> 4 drop duplicate id+time 24663    3747







ImportantAlways produce this table



It goes in your methods section, and it is the first thing a reviewer — or a future you — will want. “We removed 3,747 duplicated records (13.2%)” is a sentence you can defend. “We cleaned the data” is not.



trk <- make_track(clean, x, y, t, id = id, crs = 4326) |>
  transform_coords(crs_to = 32736)

trk

2a. What is the programmed fix interval? 2b. Why is the mean so much larger than the median? 2c. Which individual has the worst gap, and how long is it in days?

The median is 1 hour for every animal — that is the schedule. The mean is inflated by a handful of enormous gaps:

gaps <- trk |>

  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>

  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(
    median_dt = median(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_dt   = round(mean(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
    max_gap_days = round(max(dt_h, na.rm = TRUE) / 24, 1),

text:
Task 3 — Hunt the speed outliers
First, look. Then delete.

steps_raw <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t_, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    dt_h = as.numeric(difftime(t_, lag(t_), units = "hours")),
    dist_m = sqrt((x_ - lag(x_))^2 + (y_ - lag(y_))^2),
    speed_kmh = (dist_m / 1000) / dt_h
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(!is.na(speed_kmh))

summary(steps_raw$speed_kmh)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>  0.00000  0.03129  0.15101  0.29545  0.38204 63.10252
sum(steps_raw$speed_kmh > 15)
#> [1] 4

Your turn
3a. Look at the fastest steps. Are they long or are they brief?






NoteSolution






steps_raw |>
  slice_max(speed_kmh, n = 10) |>
  transmute(id, t_, dt_min = round(dt_h * 60, 1),
            dist_m = round(dist_m), speed_kmh = round(speed_kmh))
#> # A tibble: 10 × 5
#>    id     t_                  dt_min dist_m speed_kmh
#>  * <chr>  <dttm>               <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 Toni   2006-04-20 19:10:00     60  63103        63
#>  2 Toni   2006-04-20 18:10:00     61  63067        62
#>  3 Pepper 2006-05-24 05:06:00     60  17379        17
#>  4 Pepper 2006-05-24 06:07:00     61  16804        17
#>  5 Cilla  2005-07-14 05:35:00     60  13386        13
#>  6 Queen  2005-09-15 07:41:00     70  11783        10
#>  7 Pepper 2006-05-23 15:06:00     60   9898        10
#>  8 Queen  2006-05-26 04:16:00      2    314         9
#>  9 Pepper 2005-10-21 23:02:00      3    255         5
#> 10 Queen  2005-03-26 00:00:00     60   4728         5

The worst offenders have tiny time gaps, not large distances — a couple of hundred metres over a minute or two. These are near-duplicate transmissions that survived the exact-duplicate filter.
Confirm it across all the fast steps:

fast <- steps_raw |> filter(speed_kmh > 15)
summary(fast$dt_h * 60)     # minutes
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>    60.0    60.0    60.5    60.5    61.0    61.0
summary(fast$dist_m)        # metres
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   16804   17235   40223   40088   63076   63103


plot(steps_raw$dt_h * 60, steps_raw$speed_kmh, log = "xy",
     pch = 16, cex = 0.25, col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.25),
     xlab = "Time gap (minutes, log)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "Fast steps are short-interval steps")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)







The diagonal edge is the signature: apparent speed is bounded by (GPS error)/dt, so as dt shrinks, apparent speed explodes. This is a time problem masquerading as a speed problem — and deleting the “fast” fixes would remove perfectly good locations.
The correct remedy is to resample onto a regular grid, which is Task 4.

title: Exercise 3 — Clean, resample and map a track
text:
Task 4 — Resample into bursts
This is where almost everyone writes a silent bug. Try the obvious thing first.

# The "obvious" pipeline — grouped by individual
naive <- trk |>
  group_by(id) |>
  track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) |>
  ungroup()

nrow(trk)
#> [1] 24663
nrow(naive)
#> [1] 10395
naive |> count(id, name = "kept")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 2
#>   id      kept
#>   <chr>  <int>
#> 1 Cilla   2731
#> 2 Gabs    1921
#> 3 Mvubu    166
#> 4 Pepper   644
#> 5 Queen   1741
#> 6 Toni    3192







Importanttrack_resample() does not respect group_by()



Look at the per-animal counts. Mvubu goes from 2,572 fixes to a couple of hundred — but Mvubu’s data are fine: 98.8% of that animal’s intervals are within 10 minutes of one hour.
track_resample() walks the rows in time order and builds one grid across everything you hand it. With six animals interleaved, fixes from animal B fall between the grid points of animal A, and most of the track is discarded. No error. No warning. Just a much smaller dataset.


The documented amt idiom is to split, resample each animal separately, and recombine:

library(tidyr)

trk_hr <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) {
    d |>
      track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(10)) |>
      filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)
  })) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

nrow(trk_hr)
#> [1] 22828


trk |> count(id, name = "before") |>
  left_join(naive   |> count(id, name = "grouped_WRONG"), by = "id") |>
  left_join(trk_hr  |> count(id, name = "nested_right"), by = "id") |>
  mutate(pct_kept = round(100 * nested_right / before, 1))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   id     before grouped_WRONG nested_right pct_kept
#> * <chr>   <int>         <int>        <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla    3528          2731         3518     99.7
#> 2 Gabs     3670          1921         3562     97.1
#> 3 Mvubu    2572           166         2544     98.9
#> 4 Pepper   4571           644         3086     67.5
#> 5 Queen    4545          1741         4354     95.8
#> 6 Toni     5777          3192         5764     99.8

Now we keep ~93% of the fixes, which is what an hourly schedule with occasional failures should give.
Your turn
4a. Recompute speeds on the correctly resampled track. Did the problem go away? 4b. What happens if you set tolerance = minutes(1)?






NoteSolution






st <- trk_hr |> steps_by_burst()

summary(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>      54      60      60      60      60      70

sp <- (st$sl_ / 1000) / as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "hours")
round(quantile(sp, c(0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, 1)), 2)
#>   50%   90%   99% 99.9%  100% 
#>  0.15  0.73  1.93  3.05 63.10
sum(sp > 15)
#> [1] 4

Every step now spans 50–70 minutes, and the time-artefact speeds are gone: the median is a few hundred metres per hour, which is what a buffalo does.
But a handful of steps remain absurdly fast. These are different animals entirely — look at them:

st[sp > 15, c("t1_", "sl_", "dt_")] |> head(5)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   t1_                    sl_ dt_    
#> * <dttm>               <dbl> <drtn> 
#> 1 2006-04-20 17:09:00 63067. 61 mins
#> 2 2006-04-20 18:10:00 63103. 60 mins
#> 3 2006-05-24 04:06:00 17379. 60 mins
#> 4 2006-05-24 05:06:00 16804. 61 mins

Sixty-five kilometres in an hour. That is not a short time gap; it is a genuine spatial outlier — a corrupt fix that teleported the animal and back. Now that every step spans the same interval, a fast step really does mean a long distance, and a speed filter finally does what you meant it to do.

plot(as.numeric(st$dt_, units = "mins"), sp, log = "y", pch = 16, cex = 0.3,
     col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.3),
     xlab = "Step duration (minutes)", ylab = "Speed km/h (log)",
     main = "After resampling: fast = far, not brief")
abline(h = 15, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)







Compare this with the plot in Task 3: the diagonal artefact edge has gone, and what is left above the line is a small, isolated cluster of real errors.

tight <- trk |>
  nest(data = -id) |>
  mutate(data = lapply(data, \(d) d |>
    track_resample(rate = hours(1), tolerance = minutes(1)) |>
    filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3))) |>
  unnest(cols = data)

c(tolerance_10min = nrow(trk_hr), tolerance_1min = nrow(tight))
#> tolerance_10min  tolerance_1min 
#>           22828           21903

A tight tolerance discards fixes that arrived a few minutes late — real data you would rather keep. A loose one lets “hourly” steps range from 40 to 80 minutes, weakening every step-length comparison. 5–10% of the interval is a reasonable compromise; state whichever you chose.

title: Exercise 3 — Clean, resample and map a track
text:
Self-check

Which cleaning order is correct?

Speed filter → remove duplicates → resample
Remove duplicates → resample to a regular rate → inspect remaining outliers
Resample → remove duplicates → speed filter
The order does not matter


Duplicates and near-duplicates create tiny time gaps, and tiny time gaps create enormous apparent speeds. Filter on speed first and you delete good fixes for a fault that belongs to their neighbours.
Remove duplicates, then resample so that every step spans a comparable interval, and then look at what is still implausible. By that point, a genuinely fast step really is a long distance.



You pipe six animals into group_by(id) |> track_resample(rate = hours(1)) and keep 42% of your fixes. The same animals resampled one at a time keep 93%. Why?

track_resample() ignores group_by() and builds one time grid across all animals
group_by() removed the duplicate timestamps
The tolerance was too tight
42% is correct; the per-animal version double-counts


track_resample() walks the rows in time order and lays a single regular grid over whatever you give it. Hand it six interleaved animals and most fixes fall between grid points set by some other individual, so they are dropped.
It fails silently — no error, no warning, just a smaller dataset — which is what makes it dangerous. Use the nest() / lapply() / unnest() idiom so each animal gets its own grid.
The general lesson: not every function respects dplyr grouping. When a step drops far more data than you expected, check the per-group counts before you accept the result.

text:
Goals. Build an sf object from a CSV; reproject it; measure distances correctly (and incorrectly, so you can see the difference); read a real raster and sample it at your fixes; make an undistorted map.
Time: ~50 minutes. Packages: sf, terra, dplyr.
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(dplyr)

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
section: Task 1 — From data frame to sf
text:
Task 1 — From data frame to sf


buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz") |>
  transmute(
    id = individual.local.identifier,
    t  = as.POSIXct(timestamp, tz = "UTC"),
    lon = location.long,
    lat = location.lat
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(lon), !is.na(lat)) |>
  distinct(id, t, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  arrange(id, t)

nrow(buffalo)
#> [1] 24663

buf_sf <- st_as_sf(buffalo, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE)
buf_sf
#> Simple feature collection with 24663 features and 4 fields
#> Geometry type: POINT
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: 31.58639 ymin: -25.16421 xmax: 32.35671 ymax: -23.99802
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#> First 10 features:
#>       id                   t      lon       lat                   geometry
#> 1  Cilla 2005-07-14 04:35:00 31.80449 -25.06147 POINT (31.80449 -25.06147)
#> 2  Cilla 2005-07-14 05:35:00 31.88776 -24.96738 POINT (31.88776 -24.96738)
#> 3  Cilla 2005-07-14 07:35:00 31.85942 -24.94288 POINT (31.85942 -24.94288)
#> 4  Cilla 2005-07-14 08:34:00 31.85512 -24.94914 POINT (31.85512 -24.94914)
#> 5  Cilla 2005-07-14 09:35:00 31.85694 -24.95424 POINT (31.85694 -24.95424)
#> 6  Cilla 2005-07-14 10:35:00 31.85977 -24.94735 POINT (31.85977 -24.94735)
#> 7  Cilla 2005-07-14 11:34:00 31.84466 -24.93435 POINT (31.84466 -24.93435)
#> 8  Cilla 2005-07-14 12:35:00 31.84410 -24.93400    POINT (31.8441 -24.934)
#> 9  Cilla 2005-07-14 13:34:00 31.84463 -24.93442 POINT (31.84463 -24.93442)
#> 10 Cilla 2005-07-14 14:35:00 31.85700 -24.93371   POINT (31.857 -24.93371)







Tip



remove = FALSE keeps the original lon/lat columns. Handy — you often want the plain numbers alongside the geometry.


Your turn
1a. What does st_crs(buf_sf) report? Find the EPSG code and the units. 1b. What is the bounding box?






NoteSolution






st_crs(buf_sf)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
st_crs(buf_sf)$units_gdal
#> [1] "degree"
st_is_longlat(buf_sf)
#> [1] TRUE

st_bbox(buf_sf)
#>      xmin      ymin      xmax      ymax 
#>  31.58639 -25.16421  32.35671 -23.99802

Degrees, EPSG:4326, and st_is_longlat() is TRUE — the flag that should make you stop before computing any distance or area.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
section: Task 2 — Reproject, and watch the numbers change
text:
Task 2 — Reproject, and watch the numbers change
Kruger sits in UTM zone 36S, EPSG:32736.

buf_utm <- st_transform(buf_sf, 32736)

# Same animal, same fix, different numbers
st_coordinates(buf_sf)[1, ]
#>         X         Y 
#>  31.80449 -25.06147
st_coordinates(buf_utm)[1, ]
#>         X         Y 
#>  379415.9 7227712.7







ImportantWhich zone?



zone = floor((longitude + 180) / 6) + 1. Kruger is at ~31.8°E, so floor(211.8 / 6) + 1 = 36. Southern hemisphere → EPSG 327 + zone = 32736. Northern would be 326 + zone.


Your turn
2a. Confirm the round trip: transform back to 4326 and compare to the original.






NoteSolution






back <- st_transform(buf_utm, 4326)
max(abs(st_coordinates(back) - st_coordinates(buf_sf)))
#> [1] 1.776357e-14

Agreement to ~1e-9 degrees — about 0.1 mm. Reprojection is lossless up to floating-point precision; it is not a source of error you need to worry about.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
section: Task 3 — Three ways to measure one distance
text:
Task 3 — Three ways to measure one distance
Take the first two fixes of buffalo “Queen” and measure the step three ways.

queen <- buf_sf |> filter(id == "Queen") |> slice(1:2)

# (1) WRONG — Euclidean on degrees, pretending they are metres
xy <- st_coordinates(queen)
wrong <- sqrt(diff(xy[, 1])^2 + diff(xy[, 2])^2)
wrong
#> [1] 0.002835514

# (2) Geodesic on the ellipsoid — sf does this automatically for 4326
geodesic <- st_distance(queen[1, ], queen[2, ])
geodesic
#> Units: [m]
#>          [,1]
#> [1,] 301.4658

# (3) Euclidean in projected metres
queen_utm <- st_transform(queen, 32736)
projected <- st_distance(queen_utm[1, ], queen_utm[2, ])
projected
#> Units: [m]
#>          [,1]
#> [1,] 300.9957

Your turn
3a. Explain the three numbers. 3b. How big is the disagreement between (2) and (3), in relative terms?






NoteSolution






c(wrong_degrees = as.numeric(wrong),
  geodesic_m    = as.numeric(geodesic),
  projected_m   = as.numeric(projected))
#> wrong_degrees    geodesic_m   projected_m 
#>  2.835514e-03  3.014658e+02  3.009957e+02

# Relative difference between the two *correct* methods
abs(as.numeric(geodesic) - as.numeric(projected)) / as.numeric(geodesic)
#> [1] 0.001559558

Number (1) is in degrees and is not a distance at all — it is a dimensionless mix of two different angular units. It is small not because the animal barely moved, but because degrees are big.
Numbers (2) and (3) are both in metres and agree to a small fraction of a percent. That is UTM doing its job: inside one zone, distortion is under 0.1%.
Practical rule. For distances, either is fine inside a zone. But for kernel density, step-length distributions, buffers and anything involving area, project first — those methods assume a plane.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
section: Task 4 — Scale up: all steps for all animals
text:
Task 4 — Scale up: all steps for all animals

step_lengths <- buf_utm |>
  group_by(id) |>
  arrange(t, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    sl = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, lag(geometry), by_element = TRUE)),
    dt = as.numeric(difftime(t, lag(t), units = "hours"))
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(sl))

summary(step_lengths$sl)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#>     0.00    28.54   153.92   330.34   399.99 63102.52

Your turn
4a. What is the median step length per individual? 4b. Plot the distribution of step lengths. Why the long tail?






NoteSolution






step_lengths |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_sl = median(sl), max_sl = max(sl), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   id         n median_sl max_sl
#>   <chr>  <int>     <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 Cilla   3527      149. 13386.
#> 2 Gabs    3669      107.  6112.
#> 3 Mvubu   2571      127.  6114.
#> 4 Pepper  4570      181. 21244.
#> 5 Queen   4544      171. 16082.
#> 6 Toni    5776      174. 63103.


par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(step_lengths$sl, breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "Step lengths", xlab = "metres")
hist(log10(step_lengths$sl + 1), breaks = 60, col = "#1f6f78", border = "white",
     main = "log10(step length + 1)", xlab = "log10 metres")






par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Two things produce the tail. First, genuine long movements. Second — and this is the important one — steps separated by long time gaps. A “step” across a 12-hour gap is not comparable to a step across one hour.

plot(step_lengths$dt, step_lengths$sl, pch = 16, cex = 0.2,
     col = adjustcolor("#1f6f78", 0.3), log = "y",
     xlab = "Time gap (hours)", ylab = "Step length (m), log scale")







Step length is meaningless without its time interval. This is why Class 3 resamples tracks to a regular interval before computing anything.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
text:
Task 5 — A real raster
We use SRTM-derived elevation for the Kruger area, already cropped for you.

elev <- rast("data/kruger_elevation.tif")
elev
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 168, 132, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.008333333, 0.008333333  (x, y)
#> extent      : 31.4, 32.5, -25.3, -23.9  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : lon/lat WGS 84 (EPSG:4326)
#> source      : kruger_elevation.tif
#> name        : elevation
#> min value   :       117
#> max value   :       572

Your turn
5a. What is the resolution, in degrees and roughly in metres? 5b. Extract elevation at every buffalo fix. What is the range?






NoteSolution






res(elev)                       # degrees
#> [1] 0.008333333 0.008333333
res(elev)[2] * 111320           # metres, north-south
#> [1] 927.6667
res(elev)[1] * 111320 * cos(24.5 * pi / 180)   # metres, east-west
#> [1] 844.1407

crs(elev, describe = TRUE)$code
#> [1] "4326"

30 arc-seconds ≈ 900 m. The raster is in EPSG:4326, the same CRS as buf_sf — so we extract with the geographic version, not the UTM one.

buf_sf$elevation <- terra::extract(elev, vect(buf_sf))[, "elevation"]

summary(buf_sf$elevation)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
#>   148.0   239.0   265.0   260.5   287.0   422.0       1
sum(is.na(buf_sf$elevation))
#> [1] 1


boxplot(elevation ~ id, data = st_drop_geometry(buf_sf),
        col = "#1f6f78", border = "grey30",
        xlab = "", ylab = "Elevation (m)",
        main = "Elevation used, by individual")







Individuals occupy noticeably different elevation bands — a first hint that they are not interchangeable, and a preview of Class 7.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
text:
Task 6 — Deliberately break it
Do this on purpose, once, so you recognise the symptom for the rest of your career.

elev_utm <- project(elev, "EPSG:32736")

First, the good news. Both objects carry a CRS, so terra sorts it out itself — note the warning it prints:

ok <- terra::extract(elev_utm, vect(buf_sf))
mean(is.na(ok[, 2]))
#> [1] 4.054657e-05

Now the bad news. Strip the coordinates down to a bare matrix and the CRS goes with them:

xy <- st_coordinates(buf_sf)          # just numbers — no CRS attached
bad <- terra::extract(elev_utm, xy)
mean(is.na(bad[, 1]))
#> [1] 1

Every value is NA. No error, no warning — just a column of missing data that would quietly propagate into your model.
Your turn
6a. Explain why. 6b. Find the second way to produce the same failure.






NoteSolution





A matrix has no CRS, so terra can only assume the numbers are already in the raster’s coordinate system. It reads longitude 31.8 as 31.8 metres east of the UTM 36S origin — a point in the Gulf of Guinea, far outside the extent:

ext(elev_utm)
#> SpatExtent : 337122.45809718, 449698.040805795, 7201293.28983987, 7356754.80881844 (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
apply(xy, 2, range)
#>             X         Y
#> [1,] 31.58639 -25.16421
#> [2,] 32.35671 -23.99802

The second route to the same failure is an object whose CRS is undefined:

elev_nocrs <- elev_utm
crs(elev_nocrs) <- ""
worse <- terra::extract(elev_nocrs, vect(buf_sf))
mean(is.na(worse[, 2]))
#> [1] 1

Now terra has nothing to transform to, so it assumes agreement — and fails the same silent way.









WarningThe habit to build





Keep coordinates inside objects that carry a CRS (sf, SpatVector). Do not pass bare matrices around.
When terra prints transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster, that is not noise — it is telling you your inputs disagreed. Read it.
Before every extract(), ten seconds of checking:

crs(r, describe = TRUE)$code ; st_crs(pts)$epsg    # same code?
ext(r) ; st_bbox(pts)                              # overlapping numbers?

section: Task 7 — A map that is not distorted
text:
Task 7 — A map that is not distorted

elev_crop <- crop(elev, ext(st_bbox(buf_sf)) + 0.05)

plot(elev_crop, col = hcl.colors(50, "Terrain2"),
     main = "Buffalo tracks over elevation, Kruger NP",
     plg = list(title = "m a.s.l."))

ids <- unique(buf_sf$id)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(ids), "Dark 3")
for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
  d <- buf_sf[buf_sf$id == ids[i], ]
  lines(st_coordinates(d), col = adjustcolor(cols[i], 0.8), lwd = 1)
}
legend("topright", legend = ids, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)













NoteWhy this one is not distorted





terra::plot() reads the CRS and, for geographic coordinates, sets the aspect ratio to 1/cos(latitude) so that a kilometre east looks like a kilometre north. Compare with last week’s plot(..., asp = 1), which did not.
You can check what it used:

p <- plot(elev_crop); 1 / cos(mean(c(-25.3, -23.9)) * pi / 180)
#> [1] 1.099824




Your turn
7a. Save the buffalo points as a GeoPackage and read them back.






NoteSolution






f <- file.path(tempdir(), "buffalo.gpkg")
st_write(buf_sf, f, delete_dsn = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)

again <- st_read(f, quiet = TRUE)
st_crs(again)$epsg
#> [1] 4326
nrow(again)
#> [1] 24663

Use GeoPackage (.gpkg), not shapefile. Shapefiles truncate column names to 10 characters, cannot store POSIXct properly, are limited to 2 GB, and are actually 4+ files that people lose track of. GeoPackage is one file, one standard, no surprises.

title: Exercise 2 — sf, terra and coordinate reference systems
text:
Self-check

st_crs(x) <- 32736 on an object whose coordinates are longitude/latitude. What have you done?

Reprojected the data to UTM 36S
Mislabelled the data — the coordinates are unchanged but now claimed to be metres
Nothing; sf ignores invalid assignments
Produced an error


Assigning a CRS only writes a label. The numbers 31.8 and −24.5 are now interpreted as 31.8 m east and 24.5 m south of the UTM 36S origin — a point in the Atlantic off West Africa.
It fails silently, which is what makes it dangerous. st_transform() is the function that changes coordinates.



Which CRS would you use to compute home-range areas for Leo the vulture, whose track spans 7°N to 54°N and 108°W to 68°W?

EPSG:32613 (UTM zone 13N), where he was tagged
EPSG:3857 (Web Mercator)
An equal-area projection appropriate to the Americas, or per-season UTM zones after segmenting
EPSG:4326 — sf computes geodesic areas anyway


A single UTM zone is 6° wide; Leo spans about 40° of longitude, so distortion far from zone 13 is severe. Web Mercator is conformal and not equal-area — areas at 54°N are inflated by roughly a factor of three relative to the equator, so it is the worst possible choice for comparing areas.
The right answers are an equal-area CRS covering the Americas, or — better — to segment first (Class 6) and estimate separate ranges for the breeding and wintering areas, each in its own local projection. A single range for this animal is not a meaningful quantity, whatever CRS you use.
sf does compute geodesic areas on 4326, but kernel density estimators need projected coordinates regardless.

title: Exercise 1 — First contact with a track
text:
Task 1 — Read the data
R reads gzipped CSV directly. No need to decompress anything.

buffalo <- read.csv("data/buffalo_kruger.csv.gz", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

dim(buffalo)
#> [1] 28410    18
names(buffalo)
#>  [1] "event.id"                        "visible"                        
#>  [3] "timestamp"                       "location.long"                  
#>  [5] "location.lat"                    "behavioural.classification"     
#>  [7] "comments"                        "manually.marked.outlier"        
#>  [9] "sensor.type"                     "individual.taxon.canonical.name"
#> [11] "tag.local.identifier"            "individual.local.identifier"    
#> [13] "study.name"                      "utm.easting"                    
#> [15] "utm.northing"                    "utm.zone"                       
#> [17] "study.timezone"                  "study.local.timestamp"







NoteWhy did the column names change?





Movebank uses hyphens: location-long. R identifiers cannot contain hyphens, so read.csv() converts them to dots by default: location.long. You can keep the originals with check.names = FALSE, but then you need backticks everywhere — not worth it.



Your turn
1a. How many rows? How many columns? 1b. How many individual animals, and what are they called? 1c. What species, and what sensor type?






NoteSolution






nrow(buffalo)
#> [1] 28410
ncol(buffalo)
#> [1] 18

unique(buffalo$individual.local.identifier)
#> [1] "Queen"  "Gabs"   "Cilla"  "Mvubu"  "Toni"   "Pepper"
length(unique(buffalo$individual.local.identifier))
#> [1] 6

unique(buffalo$individual.taxon.canonical.name)
#> [1] "Syncerus caffer"
unique(buffalo$sensor.type)
#> [1] "gps"

Six buffalo, GPS-collared. Note that table() is more informative than unique() when you also want the number of fixes per animal:

table(buffalo$individual.local.identifier)
#> 
#>  Cilla   Gabs  Mvubu Pepper  Queen   Toni 
#>   3556   4831   3491   5163   4997   6372

Already a lesson: the animals are not equally sampled. Any summary that pools them without accounting for that is dominated by whichever individual contributed most fixes.

title: Exercise 1 — First contact with a track
text:
Task 2 — Timestamps are not text
This is the single most important line of code in the whole course.

buffalo$t <- as.POSIXct(buffalo$timestamp, format = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S", tz = "UTC")

class(buffalo$t)
#> [1] "POSIXct" "POSIXt"
range(buffalo$t)
#> [1] "2005-02-17 05:05:00 UTC" "2006-12-31 14:34:00 UTC"







WarningAlways set tz



If you omit tz, R silently uses your computer’s time zone. Your analysis then gives different answers on a laptop in Rome and a server in California. Movebank timestamps are UTC. Say so.


Your turn
2a. Over how many days does the study run? 2b. In which months are there most fixes?






NoteSolution






difftime(max(buffalo$t), min(buffalo$t), units = "days")
#> Time difference of 682.3951 days

table(format(buffalo$t, "%Y-%m"))
#> 
#> 2005-02 2005-03 2005-04 2005-05 2005-06 2005-07 2005-08 2005-09 2005-10 2005-11 
#>     289     752    1290     887     889    1190    3220    4186    4192    3704 
#> 2005-12 2006-01 2006-02 2006-03 2006-04 2006-05 2006-06 2006-07 2006-08 2006-09 
#>    2574    1425     841     737     626     582     235     197     147     138 
#> 2006-10 2006-11 2006-12 
#>     108     140      61

The monthly counts are very uneven — collars were deployed and failed at different times. This matters: a “seasonal” pattern can easily be a deployment pattern in disguise.

Task 3 — Subset one animal and sort it
Almost every movement calculation assumes the rows are one individual, in time order. Never assume a file arrives sorted.

queen <- buffalo[buffalo$individual.local.identifier == "Queen", ]
queen <- queen[order(queen$t), ]

nrow(queen)
#> [1] 4997
head(queen[, c("t", "location.long", "location.lat")])
#>                     t location.long location.lat
#> 1 2005-02-17 05:05:00      31.76642    -24.53730
#> 2 2005-02-17 05:05:00      31.76642    -24.53730
#> 3 2005-02-17 06:08:00      31.76442    -24.53931
#> 4 2005-02-17 06:08:00      31.76442    -24.53931
#> 5 2005-02-17 07:05:00      31.76114    -24.54799
#> 6 2005-02-17 08:05:00      31.76080    -24.54703

Your turn
3a. Were the rows already in time order? 3b. Are there repeated timestamps?






NoteSolution






# Was the original order already sorted in time?
queen_raw <- buffalo[buffalo$individual.local.identifier == "Queen", ]
is.unsorted(queen_raw$t)
#> [1] FALSE

# Repeated timestamps?
sum(duplicated(queen$t))
#> [1] 452

There are duplicated timestamps — the collar transmitted the same fix more than once. Across the whole file:

sum(duplicated(buffalo[, c("individual.local.identifier", "timestamp")]))
#> [1] 3747

Roughly 13% of the file. We will remove these properly in Class 3; today just register that real data arrive dirty, and that you only find out by looking.

title: Exercise 1 — First contact with a track
section: Task 4 — Fix interval and fix success
text:
Task 4 — Fix interval and fix success
The collar was programmed to attempt a fix on a schedule. What did it actually deliver?

# Drop duplicated timestamps first, or every duplicate creates a zero-length interval
queen_u <- queen[!duplicated(queen$t), ]

dt <- as.numeric(diff(queen_u$t), units = "hours")

summary(dt)
#>      Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max. 
#> 3.333e-02 1.000e+00 1.000e+00 2.445e+00 1.000e+00 2.523e+03

Your turn
4a. What is the modal (most common) interval? That is the programmed fix rate. 4b. What fraction of intervals are exactly that? This is your fix success rate. 4c. What is the longest gap, and what might explain it?






NoteSolution






# Round to the nearest 0.1 h so near-identical intervals group together
tab <- sort(table(round(dt, 1)), decreasing = TRUE)
head(tab, 5)
#> 
#>    1  0.9    0    2  0.1 
#> 4203  120   55   42   35

modal_dt <- as.numeric(names(tab)[1])
modal_dt
#> [1] 1

# Proportion of intervals at the programmed rate
mean(abs(dt - modal_dt) < 0.1)
#> [1] 0.9515845

# The worst gap, in days
max(dt) / 24
#> [1] 105.1167

The modal interval is the programmed schedule. Everything longer is a missed fix — the collar tried and failed, or was off.
Long gaps have mundane explanations that matter enormously: battery saving schedules, the animal under dense canopy or in a gorge, the collar temporarily upside-down, or the animal dead and the collar lying face-down.
A cleaner way to count missed fixes — how many scheduled attempts fit in each observed gap:

missed <- round(dt / modal_dt) - 1
sum(missed)
#> [1] 6563
sum(missed) / (nrow(queen_u) + sum(missed))   # overall failure rate
#> [1] 0.5908354

Task 5 — Your first trajectory plot
No spatial packages. Just points and lines.

plot(queen_u$location.long, queen_u$location.lat,
     type = "l", col = "grey60",
     xlab = "Longitude (°)", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Buffalo 'Queen', Kruger NP",
     asp = 1)
points(queen_u$location.long, queen_u$location.lat,
       pch = 16, cex = 0.3, col = "#1f6f78")
points(queen_u$location.long[1], queen_u$location.lat[1],
       pch = 17, cex = 1.6, col = "forestgreen")     # start
points(tail(queen_u$location.long, 1), tail(queen_u$location.lat, 1),
       pch = 15, cex = 1.6, col = "firebrick")       # end
legend("topright", c("start", "end"), pch = c(17, 15),
       col = c("forestgreen", "firebrick"), bty = "n")













ImportantThis plot is wrong, and knowing why is the point



asp = 1 forces one degree of longitude to occupy the same screen distance as one degree of latitude. On the ground at 24°S, one degree of latitude is about 111 km, but one degree of longitude is only about 101 km — the map is stretched east–west by roughly a factor of 1.1.
At 24° the distortion is modest. Try the same plot for the vulture, which ranges from 7°N to 54°N, and it becomes severe.
Distances computed from raw degrees are meaningless. Fixing this — properly, with coordinate reference systems — is Class 2.


Your turn
5a. Plot all six buffalo on one figure, one colour each.






NoteSolution






b <- buffalo[!duplicated(buffalo[, c("individual.local.identifier", "timestamp")]), ]
ids <- unique(b$individual.local.identifier)
cols <- hcl.colors(length(ids), "Dark 3")

plot(b$location.long, b$location.lat, type = "n", asp = 1,
     xlab = "Longitude (°)", ylab = "Latitude (°)",
     main = "Six buffalo, Kruger National Park")

for (i in seq_along(ids)) {
  d <- b[b$individual.local.identifier == ids[i], ]
  d <- d[order(d$t), ]
  lines(d$location.long, d$location.lat, col = cols[i], lwd = 1)
}
legend("topleft", legend = ids, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)







The individuals overlap heavily but are not identical — the raw material of every question in this course. Do they use the same areas at the same times? Do they avoid each other? Do they respond to the same rivers?

title: Exercise 1 — First contact with a track
text:
Self-check

You compute diff(t) on a data frame you forgot to sort by time. What do you get?

An error
A mixture of positive and negative intervals, and nonsense summaries
Correct intervals — diff() sorts internally
All zeros


diff() does exactly what you asked: it subtracts each element from the next, in the order given. Out of order, you get negative time differences, and any speed you compute from them is garbage — often silently, because summary() still returns numbers.
Always order(t) within individual before any step calculation. This is the most common error in beginner movement code.



A collar programmed for hourly fixes returns 14,000 fixes over exactly two years. Roughly what was the fix success rate?

~100%
~80%
~50%
Impossible to say without the DOP values


Two years of hourly attempts is 2 × 365 × 24 ≈ 17,520. So 14,000 / 17,520 ≈ 80%, which is a fairly typical figure for a GPS collar on a large mammal in mixed habitat.
The 20% that failed is not noise: if failures concentrate in closed habitat, your data under-represent exactly the places the animal may prefer.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: Movement is the link between an animal and its environment
text:
Movement is the link between an animal and its environment
Almost every process a conservation biologist cares about is a movement process in disguise:

Gene flow — dispersal distances set population connectivity
Disease spread — contact rates are an outcome of where animals go
Population persistence — can individuals reach the next patch?
Human–wildlife conflict — where do animals and people overlap, and when?
Protected-area design — a reserve that does not contain the movements it was drawn for does not work
Climate response — range shifts are dispersal events, one individual at a time



If you cannot describe how an organism moves, you cannot predict how it will respond to a changing landscape.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
The data deluge

Trend of “movement-related” package downloads from CRAN
The constraint has moved. It used to be getting locations. It is now knowing what to do with them.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
The movement ecology paradigm
Nathan et al. (2008) reduced the whole field to four questions about every movement path:

Why move? — the internal state. Hunger, thirst, reproduction, fear. The motivation.
How to move? — the motion capacity. Legs, wings, fins; the biomechanical envelope.
When and where to move? — the navigation capacity. Memory, senses, cues, orientation.
What external factors? — the environment. Landscape, weather, predators, other individuals, people.



\(U_t = f(\Omega, \Phi, r_t, w_t)\) — the observed path is the joint outcome of all four. This is why a track is hard to interpret: many different combinations produce similar-looking paths.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Lagrangian vs Eulerian


Lagrangian
Follow the individual.
Telemetry, biologging, mark-recapture.
“Where did animal #7 go?”
Gives you the process: the sequence of decisions.

Eulerian
Watch a fixed place.
Camera traps, transects, counts, eDNA.
“How many animals passed this point?”
Gives you the pattern: density in space.


This course is almost entirely Lagrangian — but remember the two are linked: a distribution is what you get when you integrate movement over time.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Vocabulary — get this right now







Term
Meaning




Fix (or relocation)
One estimated location with a timestamp. The atom of everything.


Track / trajectory
An ordered sequence of fixes for one individual


Burst
A stretch of a track with regular sampling and no big gaps


Step
The straight segment between two consecutive fixes


Step length (SL)
Distance of a step. Note: not distance travelled


Turning angle (TA)
Change of direction between consecutive steps


Fix rate / sampling interval
How often the tag tries to locate


Fix success rate
Fraction of attempts that produced a location


Deployment
One tag, on one animal, over one period





A track is not the path the animal walked. It is a sample of that path. Everything between two fixes is an assumption.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Quiz

A GPS collar is set to attempt a fix every hour. Over one day it produces 18 locations. The straight-line distances between consecutive fixes sum to 4.1 km. Which statements are true?

The animal travelled 4.1 km that day
The animal travelled at least 4.1 km that day
The fix success rate was 75%
The 6 missing fixes can be safely ignored


4.1 km is a lower bound: the animal’s real path between fixes is at least as long as the straight line, and usually much longer. Summed step length is scale-dependent — sample twice as often and it grows.
18/24 = 75% success. And the missing fixes are the opposite of ignorable: GPS failures are not random. Fixes fail under canopy, in gorges, in dense cover — exactly the habitats an animal may be selecting. Missing data are themselves an ecological signal.

Marking individuals: the cheap and enduring methods





Cyclura carinata with coloured bead tags






A Passive Integrated Transponder (PIT)




Marks give you recaptures, not tracks — two or more points separated by a long, unobserved interval. Cheap, long-lasting, and still the backbone of demographic work.

text:
Marking: from mutilation to photographs





Toe-clipping combinations (Waichman 1992)



Effective, permanent — and now ethically contested. Increasingly replaced.





Bombina spot patterns are unique



Natural markings cost the animal nothing. Photo-ID software now does the matching at scale.

text:
Photo-identification at scale

Automated recognition of individual iguanas. Image courtesy of Nathalie DuporgePattern-matching algorithms turn a shoebox of photographs into a capture–recapture dataset — for whale sharks, giraffes, newts, iguanas.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Genetic tagging

Species and locations where genetic tagging has delivered demographic insight (after Lamb et al. 2019)
Hair snags, scats, feathers: the animal is never handled. Biased towards mid-to-large mobile mammals, because that is where the money and the conflict are.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
VHF radio-telemetry





Implanted transmitter, Chilabothrus chrysogaster






Tracking on foot with a Yagi antenna




The tag emits a pulse; you find it. A location comes from homing in or from triangulation of ≥2 bearings. Tags go down to 0.2 g — nothing else reaches insects and the smallest bats.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
What triangulation actually costs you

Each bearing has error; the location error is the intersection polygon of two noisy bearings, and it grows fast with distance
Data arrive when a human is in the field — so nights, storms and weekends are systematically under-sampled
A few dozen to a few hundred fixes per animal, unevenly spaced
Cheap tags, expensive fieldwork



The bat dataset we will use in Class 3 is exactly this: 17 individuals, 1,740 fixes in total, wildly irregular. Most methods in this course assume regular sampling. Part of your training is learning to say “not with these data”.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
GPS: trilateration

The GPS constellation
Each satellite broadcasts its position and a very precise time
Distance to a satellite = (signal travel time) × c
3 satellites fix a position in principle; a 4th is needed to solve the receiver’s clock error — and more give altitude and redundancy

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: GPS in practice, on an animal
text:
GPS in practice, on an animal


What you get

Horizontal error typically 5–30 m under open sky
A quality flag: number of satellites, DOP (dilution of precision), 2D vs 3D fix
Optional altitude, speed, temperature, activity

What it costs

A cold start (no recent almanac) can take minutes and drain the battery
Canopy, canyons, burrows and water block the signal
Energy scales with fix rate — this is the central design trade-off





A male Conolophus marthae with a Wireless Sensor Node: GPS, temperature and UV

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: Getting the data off the animal
text:
Getting the data off the animal

Store-on-board — cheapest, best battery use, but you must recapture the animal. Lose the animal, lose everything.
VHF/UHF download — get close, pull the data over the air
GSM / SMS — near-live data wherever there is mobile coverage. Fails in exactly the remote places you care about.
Iridium / Argos uplink — global, live, expensive, small data volumes
Drop-off collars — timed or remotely triggered release, then go and find the collar. Elegant, and one more thing that can fail.



Ask “how will I get the data back?” before you buy the tags. This is the question most first projects get wrong.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: Argos, geolocators, and the aquatic world
text:
Argos, geolocators, and the aquatic world


Argos
Satellites measure the Doppler shift of the tag’s transmission.
Error classes 3 → B: ~250 m to >10 km.
Global, works at sea, decades of history. Still standard for sea turtles, seabirds, pinnipeds.

Geolocators (GLS)
Log light level. Day length → latitude; time of local noon → longitude.
Error 100–200 km. Useless near equinox.
But: ~0.3 g. For small migratory birds it is the only option.

Acoustic telemetry
Tag pings; fixed hydrophones listen.
You get detections at receivers, not positions — a network problem, not a trajectory problem.
Fish, sharks, invertebrates.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: Biologging: sensors that are not locations
text:
Biologging: sensors that are not locations

Tri-axial accelerometers — the workhorse. At 10–50 Hz you can classify feeding, resting, flying, and estimate energy expenditure (ODBA)
Magnetometers + gyroscopes — heading and body rotation; combined with accelerometers gives dead reckoning: a fine-scale path between GPS fixes
Pressure / depth — dive profiles
Temperature, heart rate, gut temperature — physiology in the wild
Proximity tags — who was near whom, and for how long: social networks



The frontier is not more locations. It is locations plus sensors: knowing where and what the animal was doing there. Class 6 is the statistical version of this question when all you have is the trajectory.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Quiz

You must study the migratory route of a 22 g passerine that breeds in Italy and winters somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa. Individuals return to the same nest box each spring. Which technology?

GPS/GSM collar
Light-level geolocator
Argos PTT
VHF radio-telemetry


The 5% rule decides it: the tag should stay under ~5% of body mass, so ~1.1 g here. That excludes GPS/GSM and Argos PTTs outright. VHF has no transcontinental range.
A geolocator weighs a few tenths of a gram. Its 100–200 km error would be useless for home-range work but is irrelevant for a 4,000 km migration.
And crucially: geolocators are store-on-board, so the whole design depends on the birds’ nest-box philopatry — you must recapture them. That is not a detail, it is the study.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Tag effects are real

The 5% rule (tag ≤ 5% of body mass) is a convention, not a finding. Portugal & White (2018) showed miniaturisation has not actually made published studies lighter relative to body mass.
For flying and diving animals, drag and shape matter more than mass. A streamlined 3% package can beat a bluff 1.5% one.
Documented effects: reduced breeding success, higher energy expenditure, altered diving, changed social status, injury at the attachment site.
Effects are often delayed — and studies are rarely designed to detect them.



A tagged animal is, to some degree, a modified animal. The honest position is to minimise, measure and report the effect — not to assume it away.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Ethics and permits: the checklist

Is the question worth it? Would existing data answer it?
3 Rs — replace, reduce, refine. The smallest sample that can answer the question.
Ethics approval and national/regional permits, before fieldwork. In Italy: ISPRA and regional authorisations; EU Directive 2010/63 where applicable.
Capture and handling protocol, anaesthesia where required, trained personnel.
Attachment — weak links and planned drop-offs so nothing is worn forever.
Data sensitivity — for poached species, publishing exact coordinates can be lethal. Movebank supports embargo and coarsening.
Report the effects you observed, including the animals you lost.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Quiz

Which of these is the strongest argument for choosing a 30-minute fix interval over a 5-minute one, for a study of buffalo habitat selection?

30-minute data are more accurate
It extends the deployment over a whole year, capturing seasonal variation
Statistical software cannot handle 5-minute data
30 minutes is the standard for ungulates


Fix interval is a battery decision, and therefore a decision about how long you observe. 5-minute data over six weeks and 30-minute data over a year answer different questions — and for seasonal habitat selection, the year wins.
Accuracy per fix does not change with rate. Software is not the constraint. And “it’s the standard” is never a reason — it is a description of what other people’s batteries could manage.
The real cost: coarse sampling truncates the step-length distribution. You will see this bite in Classes 4 and 8.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
section: Bias 1 — Fix success is not random
text:
Bias 1 — Fix success is not random

GPS fixes fail under dense canopy, in steep terrain, in burrows, underwater
So the fixes you have are biased towards open habitat
Then you fit a habitat-selection model and conclude the animal prefers open habitat
You have measured your collar, not your animal



Fixes are missing because of the covariate you are modelling. This is missing-not-at-random, the nastiest kind. Mitigation: stationary test collars in each habitat type, and model fix success explicitly.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Bias 2 — Location error is structured

Error is not independent white noise: it is correlated in time and correlated with habitat
A bad fix can place an animal hundreds of metres away, producing an implausible step out and an implausible step back — a spike
Naïvely, that spike inflates your speed distribution and your home range
Filtering on speed is the standard fix, but a threshold that is too aggressive deletes real fast movement



Keep the DOP / satellite-count columns. They are your evidence about which fixes to distrust. We use them in Class 3.

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Bias 3 — The sample of animals

Tagged animals are the ones you could catch: often bolder, often in accessible places, often adults, often one sex
Sample sizes are small — 6 buffalo, 1 vulture. Individual variation is large, and \(n=1\) tells you about that individual
Tags fail unevenly: animals in rough habitat lose collars more often, so late in a study your sample has drifted
Publication bias: dispersal studies report the animals that were found



Three questions for every tracking paper you read, including yours: Which animals? Which fixes? What is missing, and why?

title: Movement, and how we track animals
text:
Quiz

A study reports that collared deer “avoid dense forest”, based on GPS collars with an overall fix success of 62%. What is the first thing you should check?

Whether the sample size was large enough
Whether fix success itself differed between forest and open habitat
Whether the collars were calibrated
Whether the study was peer-reviewed


A 38% failure rate is enormous, and canopy is the classic cause of GPS failure. If the collar fails more often under trees, forest locations are under-represented in the data by construction — and “avoidance” is an artefact of the instrument.
Sample size does not help: more collars with the same bias give you a more precise wrong answer. The standard remedy is stationary test collars deployed across habitat types to estimate habitat-specific fix rates, then weight or model accordingly.

title: Spatial data in R
text:
Vector and raster


Vector
Discrete objects with coordinates.

Point — a fix, a nest, a trap
Line — a trajectory, a river, a road
Polygon — a home range, a park boundary, a lake

Each object carries an attribute table.
Exact geometry, arbitrary precision.

Raster
A regular grid of cells, each with a value.

Elevation, NDVI, temperature, land cover
Defined by origin, cell size, number of rows/cols, CRS

Continuous surfaces, fixed resolution.
Fast maths, no notion of individual objects.



Movement analysis is nearly always points (or steps) sampling rasters. That one sentence describes Classes 5, 7 and 8.

text:
Choosing the model








Question
Model




Where exactly was the animal at 08:00?
Vector (point)


What is the NDVI there?
Raster, sampled at that point


What is the park boundary?
Vector (polygon)


How far is the nearest river?
Raster (a distance surface) or vector + distance computation


How much forest within 500 m?
Raster, summarised in a buffer





The same reality can be either. A river is a line if you care about its course, and a distance-to-river raster if you care about how far the animal is from it. Choose by the operation you need, not by what the thing “is”.

title: Spatial data in R
text:
The problem
The Earth is a lumpy ellipsoid. Maps and computer screens are flat. Getting from one to the other requires choices, and every choice distorts something.

A CRS answers three questions:

What shape is the Earth? — the ellipsoid (e.g. WGS84, GRS80)
How is that shape tied to the actual planet? — the datum
How do we flatten it? — the projection (or none, if we keep angles)
crumbs: C2 · Slides — Spatial data in R

title: Spatial data in R
text:
Geographic coordinates

Longitude and latitude are angles, not distances
Latitude: angle north/south of the equator. Longitude: angle east/west of Greenwich. Units are degrees. This is what every GPS and every Movebank file gives you — usually WGS84, EPSG:4326.
crumbs: C2 · Slides — Spatial data in R

title: Spatial data in R
section: Why you cannot do arithmetic with degrees
text:
Why you cannot do arithmetic with degrees

One degree of latitude ≈ 111 km everywhere
One degree of longitude ≈ 111 km × cos(latitude)

at the equator: 111 km
at 24° (Kruger): ~102 km
at 46° (Switzerland): ~77 km
at the pole: 0 km



# WRONG — mixes two different units
sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)

Euclidean distance on longitude/latitude is meaningless. You either project to a metric CRS, or compute great-circle distances on the ellipsoid. sf does the second automatically for EPSG:4326 — which is safe, but slower, and does not fix your plots.

title: Spatial data in R
text:
Projected coordinates

Every projection preserves some properties and destroys others
Conformal keeps angles/shape (Mercator, UTM). Equal-area keeps area (Albers, Mollweide). Equidistant keeps distances from a point. No projection keeps everything.
crumbs: C2 · Slides — Spatial data in R

title: Spatial data in R
text:
UTM: the practical default

The world is cut into 60 zones, each 6° of longitude wide
Each zone gets its own transverse Mercator projection, so distortion inside a zone is small (< 0.1%)
Coordinates in metres: easting and northing
Kruger is in zone 36S → EPSG:32736
Switzerland is in zone 32N → EPSG:32632



UTM works beautifully inside one zone. Leo the vulture crosses many zones and 47° of latitude, so no single UTM zone fits him. For continental-scale tracks use an equal-area CRS suited to the region — or work in geographic coordinates with geodesic distances.

text:
Quiz

You have buffalo fixes in EPSG:4326 and you want the area of a 95% home range polygon, in km². What is the right sequence?

Compute the polygon in 4326, then convert degrees² to km²
Transform the points to EPSG:32736, compute the polygon, read the area in m²
Transform to EPSG:3857, compute the polygon, read the area in m²
Compute the polygon in 4326 — sf handles it automatically


Project first, to a CRS whose units are metres and which is appropriate for the region — UTM 36S for Kruger. Then all the geometry operations are ordinary plane geometry and areas come out in m².
There is no fixed conversion from degrees² to km²: the factor depends on latitude. Web Mercator (3857) has units of metres but is not equal-area, so areas are systematically wrong. And while sf can compute geodesic lengths and areas on 4326, kernel-density home-range estimators need projected coordinates — they assume a plane.

section: st_crs() vs st_transform() — the classic bug
text:
st_crs() vs st_transform() — the classic bug


st_crs(x) <- 32736
“These numbers were always UTM; I am just writing down the label.”
If the numbers are actually degrees, you have now lied to R. The points land near the origin off West Africa.

st_transform(x, 32736)
“These numbers are in the current CRS; compute the corresponding UTM coordinates.”
The numbers change. This is almost always what you want.



Assign a CRS only when the data arrived without one and you know what it should be. Otherwise, transform.

title: Spatial data in R
text:
Quiz

Your colleague sends a CSV of coordinates like x = 375051, y = 7285726 and says “they’re from Kruger”. What are they, and what do you do?

Longitude/latitude — use crs = 4326
UTM 36S metres — set crs = 32736 with st_as_sf(), do not transform
Web Mercator — set crs = 3857
Impossible to know


Magnitudes give it away. Longitude and latitude are bounded by ±180 and ±90, so six- and seven-digit values cannot be degrees. Values of that size in metres with a large northing are classic UTM, and Kruger is zone 36S (EPSG:32736) — the 7,285,726 m northing is the southern-hemisphere false northing at ~24.5°S.
Because the numbers are already UTM, you declare the CRS when building the sf object (crs = 32736) rather than transforming. Transforming would treat metres as degrees.
Sanity check afterwards: st_transform(x, 4326) and confirm you land at roughly 31.8°E, 24.5°S.

title: Spatial data in R
text:
Rasters and vectors must agree
Before extract(), three things must line up:

Same CRS. If both objects carry a CRS, terra transforms for you and warns. If either lacks one — a bare coordinate matrix — it assumes they match.
Overlapping extents. Non-overlap gives you a column of NA, not an error.
Appropriate resolution. Extracting a 1 km NDVI cell for a fix with 10 m GPS error is fine. Extracting a 10 m Sentinel pixel for an Argos fix with 5 km error is self-deception.



Match the resolution of your environmental data to the error of your locations. A pixel finer than your positional error adds noise, not information.

Quiz

You run terra::extract(ndvi, cbind(buffalo$lon, buffalo$lat)) and every value comes back NA. The NDVI raster is in UTM 36S. What happened?

A bare coordinate matrix carries no CRS, so terra assumed the degrees were already metres
terra always errors on a CRS mismatch, so this cannot happen
The NDVI raster is empty
You must call crop() before extract()


Modern terra is helpful when it can be: give it a SpatVector or an sf object that carries a CRS, and it transforms your points for you, printing a warning:
[extract] transforming vector data to the CRS of the raster
But a plain two-column matrix has no CRS. terra can only assume the numbers are already in the raster’s coordinate system — so 31.8 and −24.5 are read as metres, land far outside the extent, and every lookup returns NA.
The same silent failure happens if the CRS of either object is missing (crs(r) <- ""). Lesson: keep your data in objects that carry their CRS, and never strip coordinates down to a bare matrix just to pass them along.

section: The four things that are always wrong
text:
The four things that are always wrong

Duplicated fixes — same individual, same timestamp. The collar re-transmitted. ~13% of our buffalo file.
Missing coordinates — a row exists, the location failed.
Impossible locations — (0, 0), land animals at sea, points on another continent. Usually a corrupt transmission.
Speed outliers — a fix that implies 200 km/h for a buffalo, then a return. A spike.



Clean in this order, and count what you remove at each step. A cleaning step that silently deletes 30% of your data has changed your study.
crumbs: C3 · Slides — Tracking data in R

title: Tracking data in R
section: Duplicates are not all the same
text:
Duplicates are not all the same

Exact duplicates — every field identical. Safe to drop.
Same timestamp, different coordinates — which is right? Keep the one with better quality (more satellites, lower DOP); if you cannot tell, keep the first and document it.
Near-duplicates — timestamps a few seconds apart. These create near-zero dt and therefore enormous apparent speeds.


# Blunt but explicit
trk |> distinct(id, t_, .keep_all = TRUE)

# move2 is more careful about the ambiguous case
move2::mt_filter_unique(x, criterion = "first")

title: Tracking data in R
text:
Speed filtering: useful and dangerous

Compute speed between consecutive fixes; drop anything above a biologically plausible maximum
Buffalo ~ 10 km/h sustained; vulture ~ 80 km/h in flight
The danger: a threshold that is too low deletes real fast movement — exactly the migration or escape events you may care about
The subtlety: one bad fix creates two fast steps (out and back). Naïve filters often delete the good neighbour instead of the bad point



Never filter silently. Plot what you are about to remove, look at it, then remove it. The sdafilter/argosfilter approach — which tests whether a point is fast and forms a spike — is better than a plain speed threshold.

title: Tracking data in R
text:
Quiz

You remove all fixes implying a speed above 15 km/h from the buffalo data, and your dataset shrinks by 0.4%. Then you compute mean daily displacement and it drops by 18%. What is the most likely explanation?

The filter worked correctly; the old value was inflated by errors
Many removed “fast” steps were actually short time gaps, not long distances
Buffalo never exceed 15 km/h so nothing real was removed
Daily displacement is unrelated to speed


Speed is distance divided by time. A pair of fixes 40 seconds apart — a near-duplicate — gives a huge apparent speed even if the animal moved 200 m. Filtering on speed therefore preferentially removes fixes with small time gaps, not fixes with large distances.
An 18% change in a summary statistic from deleting 0.4% of rows is a red flag that the filter is doing something other than what you intended.
Correct order: remove duplicates and near-duplicates first, resample to a regular interval second, and only then consider a speed filter — on steps that share a common dt.

Resampling and bursts
track_resample() keeps fixes that fall on a regular grid within a tolerance, and labels contiguous runs as bursts.

  filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3)

tolerance — how much slack. Too tight and you throw away good data; too loose and “hourly” steps are really 40–80 minutes
A burst breaks wherever a fix is missing. Steps are computed within bursts, never across a gap

title: Tracking data in R
text:
Quiz

track_resample() interpolates missing locations to give you a regular series. True or false?

True — that is what resampling means
False — it selects existing fixes and discards the rest


amt::track_resample() is a filter, not an interpolator. It walks the track and keeps the fixes that fall close enough to a regular time grid; where no fix is available, the burst simply ends. You never gain observations you did not make.
That is deliberate. Interpolating locations invents data and then feeds the invention into a model as if it were an observation, which biases step-length and turning-angle distributions towards straighter, slower movement.
If you genuinely need locations between fixes, use a model that says so — a continuous-time movement model (ctmm) or a state-space model — which gives you interpolated positions with uncertainty attached.

title: Tracking data in R
text:
Quiz

A colleague reports a mean sampling interval of 2.45 hours for a collar programmed to fix hourly. What does that number actually tell you?

The collar was reprogrammed partway through
Almost nothing about the schedule — a few very long gaps have inflated the mean
The fix success rate was about 41%
The animal was inactive, so the collar skipped fixes


The median for this collar is 1 hour — the schedule is intact. The mean is 2.45 h because the distribution has a long tail: one gap of 2,523 hours (105 days) drags it up on its own.
A mean sampling interval is a summary of your collar failures, not of your sampling design. Report the median, the maximum gap, and the number of gaps beyond some threshold.
And no, you cannot read the fix success rate off the mean. Success rate is the proportion of scheduled attempts that returned a location, which you get by dividing each gap by the modal interval and counting the misses.

text:
Today


Describe a trajectory with numbers: step length, turning angle, speed, net displacement
Why these numbers are scale-dependent

Home range: what it is, and what the estimators actually estimate
MCP, KDE and why autocorrelation broke them — AKDE
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
The step
Two consecutive fixes define a step.



Step length \(s_t = \lVert \mathbf{x}_{t+1} - \mathbf{x}_t \rVert\)
Absolute direction \(\phi_t = \operatorname{atan2}(\Delta y, \Delta x)\)
Turning angle \(\theta_t = \phi_t - \phi_{t-1}\), wrapped to \((-\pi, \pi]\)
Speed \(v_t = s_t / \Delta t\)



A turning angle needs three fixes. A step needs two. That is why filter_min_n_burst(min_n = 3) exists.




Turning angles are circular data: −179° and +179° are 2° apart, not 358°. Never take an arithmetic mean of angles.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Everything here is scale-dependent

Sample every 5 minutes: many short steps — but so short that GPS error randomises their direction
Sample hourly: clear directional persistence
Sample every 12 hours: few long steps, turning angles ≈ uniform (the animal looks like it moves at random)
Total path length grows without bound as the interval shrinks — the coastline paradox



“Mean step length” is not a property of the animal. It is a property of the animal and your sampling interval. Always report the interval alongside it, and never compare step lengths measured at different rates.
There is a sweet spot: fine enough to resolve the behaviour, coarse enough that a typical step is much longer than your GPS error.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Net squared displacement (NSD)
\[\text{NSD}(t) = \lVert \mathbf{x}_t - \mathbf{x}_0 \rVert^2\]
The squared distance from the starting point. A remarkably effective diagnostic:

Sedentary — NSD rises then plateaus at a low value
Migratory — a sigmoid up, a plateau, a sigmoid back down
Dispersal — a single step up to a new plateau
Nomadic — rises roughly linearly, no plateau



Fitting these shapes as competing non-linear models (Bunnefeld et al. 2011) is a cheap and surprisingly effective way to classify movement strategies.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Quiz

Two studies report mean step length for the same population of roe deer. Study A reports 180 m, study B reports 640 m. Both are competent. What is the most likely explanation?

Study B’s collars had worse GPS accuracy
Study B sampled at a longer interval
Study B included migratory individuals
One of them made an arithmetic error


Step length scales with the sampling interval. An animal sampled hourly produces shorter steps than the same animal sampled every four hours, because the straight line between fixes cuts across all the wiggles in between.
This is why step length is not comparable across studies unless the interval matches, and why you must state the interval in every methods section.
It is also why Class 8’s step selection functions always compare an observed step with alternatives of exactly the same duration.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Three canonical walks


Simple / BRW
Turning angles uniform; direction has no memory.
Diffusive: displacement grows as \(\sqrt{t}\).

Correlated (CRW)
Turning angles concentrated near 0; direction persists.
Locally directed, diffusive at long range.

Lévy walk
Step lengths from a heavy-tailed distribution.
Rare very long steps; super-diffusive. Much argued over.



These are null models. They tell you what a trajectory would look like if the animal responded to nothing. Departures from them are where the biology is.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Biased random walk
Add a preferred direction — towards a den, a water hole, a wintering ground — and you have a biased random walk. Combine with persistence and you get the BCRW, the workhorse null model for animals with both memory and a goal.


Class 8’s integrated step selection analysis is, in effect, a biased correlated random walk whose bias is estimated from environmental covariates. Keep that connection in mind.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
What is a home range?

“That area traversed by the individual in its normal activities of food gathering, mating and caring for young.” — Burt (1943)



Note what it excludes: exploratory forays, migration, dispersal
Note what it does not say: nothing about a probability distribution, nothing about a percentage
Powell & Mitchell (2012): a home range is a cognitive map the animal uses — and our estimators are crude proxies for it




Every estimator answers a slightly different question. “95% home range” is not a fact about the animal; it is a number produced by a method with assumptions. Say which method, and why.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
MCP — minimum convex polygon
The smallest convex polygon containing \(x\)% of the fixes.


For

Trivial to compute and explain
Comparable with a century of literature
No smoothing parameter to argue about


Against

Convex — includes land the animal never used (lakes, cliffs, cities)
Extremely sensitive to outliers and to sample size
Area grows with the number of fixes; no asymptote
No density information — every point counts the same




Use it for comparability with old studies. Do not use it as your only estimate.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
KDE — kernel density estimation
Put a small “bump” (kernel) on each fix, sum them into a utilisation distribution (UD), then draw the contour containing 95% of the volume.

Gives a density, not just a boundary — you can have disjoint core areas
The answer is dominated by the bandwidth \(h\)

href (reference) — assumes bivariate normal; usually over-smooths
hlscv (least-squares cross-validation) — often fails to converge, or fragments the UD into confetti
hpi (plug-in) — generally the most reliable default




Report your bandwidth selector. Two papers using “95% KDE” with different bandwidths are not comparable.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
section: The problem KDE has with tracking data
text:
The problem KDE has with tracking data
Classical KDE assumes fixes are independent samples from the UD.

GPS fixes an hour apart are nothing of the sort — the animal was 300 m away an hour ago and will be 300 m away in an hour.

Effective sample size is far smaller than \(n\)
So the UD is under-estimated — the home range comes out too small
And collecting more fixes at a higher rate makes it worse, not better




This is why area estimates from the 1990s (a few dozen VHF fixes) and from today (50,000 GPS fixes) are not comparable. It is not that the animals changed.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
AKDE — autocorrelated KDE
Fleming et al. (2015): first fit a continuous-time movement model to the track, estimate the autocorrelation structure, and use it to derive the effective sample size. Then do the kernel estimate.

Gives confidence intervals on the area — almost nothing else does
Handles irregular sampling gracefully
Tells you when your data are inadequate, instead of returning a confident-looking number
ctmm package; also a point-and-click web app



If you report one home-range estimate in a modern paper, make it AKDE, and report the confidence interval. If your CI spans an order of magnitude, that is the honest answer.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Quiz

You estimate a 95% KDE home range from hourly GPS data (n = 8,000) and get 12 km². A 1995 study of the same population using VHF (n = 60) reported 31 km². What is the most likely explanation?

The population’s range has genuinely shrunk by 60%
Autocorrelation in the GPS data biases classical KDE downwards
The VHF study had larger location errors, inflating the area
The two studies used different percentage contours


Classical KDE assumes independent fixes. Hourly GPS locations are strongly autocorrelated, so 8,000 fixes carry the information of perhaps a few hundred independent ones — and the estimator systematically under-estimates the range. The sparse VHF fixes, days apart, were much closer to independent.
Location error does inflate areas, but it is a far smaller effect than this.
The way to settle it is AKDE: fit the movement model, get the effective sample size, and produce an area with a confidence interval. Very often the modern estimate then agrees with the old one — and you have learned that the population did not change, your method did.
crumbs: C4 · Slides — Movement metrics & home range

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:

title: Movement metrics and home range
text:
Quiz

You compute a 100% MCP for an animal after 3 months, then again after 12 months. The area has tripled. What can you conclude?

The animal expanded its home range over the year
Very little — MCP area grows with the number of fixes and has no asymptote
The collar’s accuracy degraded
The 100% contour is invalid; use 95%


The MCP is the convex hull of your points, so every new fix can only enlarge it or leave it unchanged — never shrink it. Its area therefore increases with sample size and duration without converging, which makes comparisons across different tracking durations meaningless.
This is the single biggest problem with MCP, and it is why area-vs-sample-size curves used to be standard practice.
Dropping to 95% removes the most extreme points and helps a little, but it does not fix the underlying behaviour. A genuine expansion would need to be demonstrated with an estimator that converges — AKDE, with confidence intervals, on comparable time windows.
